title: The Most Advanced Home Device I’ve Tested This Year Is in My Garage
snippet: A Chamberlain smart garage and security system combined is the home tech I didn’t know I needed.
fullText:
Tyler Lacoma/CNET Art		

	

		

									

						Chamberlain Premier Smart Garage Door Opener with Camera					

					

	9.0

	
					

			

	

		

			

				Pros & Cons			

			

			

							

					
						Advanced smart controls with built-in security camera					
				

							

					
						Bright 2,000-lumen LED lights can replace old overhead lighting					
				

							

					
						Keypad, wall controller and remotes included					
				

							

					
						Tons of setting options to control remotely via app, set timers, set automatic garage closing rules, or create schedules					
				

							

					
						Advanced, adjustable camera with AI detection and motion zone control					
				

							

					
						1.4 HP power and new railing improved garage sound and performance, too					
				

					

			

							

					
						Not everyone wants a garage security cam, and its advanced features require a subscription					
				

							

					
						Not suitable for side-mounted garage motors					
				

					

	

		

After months of testing home artificial intelligence, new types of security cameras, the next era of sensors and a flashlight of the future, the most high-tech product of all ended up transforming my garage – and it could do the same for yours, if you’re willing to commit to an overhaul of your garage door and home security at the same time.

Chamberlain’s latest Premier Smart Garage Door Opener with MyQ technology ($379, with Chamberlain offering several similar models) isn’t just a smart garage door opener, although I came away impressed with those features. It’s also a security camera equipped with the latest AI recognition and camera technology to watch both your car and the garage door or side door, plus a super-bright LED light that can replace any other overhead garage lighting.

While so much surveillance may be overkill for some (you can, fortunately, turn off or adjust camera features as needed), the total capabilities add up to a particularly potent home upgrade.

			

More from CNET

If you’re worried about protecting your car, making sure the garage door is closed or watching especially vulnerable garage entry points, you’ll want to see what I found during my time with this all-in-one Chamberlain device.

A professional installation for a major upgrade

A smart garage may be just the unexpected smart device you need.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

I wouldn’t recommend a DIY installation of a smart garage, although technically it’s possible. The garage door itself remains unchanged, so you can keep your current look. But the motor, at least some of the railing, the aligned sensor, and the wired-in controller all need to be replaced, so it’s best to contact a professional.

In my case, it was a very good idea. Chamberlain linked me up with a local garage installer who noted that the railing included in my kit was a bit too short for my garage, and swapped it out for compatible railing that successfully fit. Installation after that was quick and smooth.

The smart garage does require a new motor, rail and sensors, but the garage door remains the same.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

In fact, it was literally smooth. The new motor and rail combination made my garage door movement far quieter and more fluid than it had ever been through years of repairs. This was an unexpected bonus of upgrading to a new setup with a 1 and ¼ HP motor.  

Operation and smart controllers

Chamberlain’s garage control options are myriad.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

How do you want to control your garage door? With this system, you can choose any option you please. I found I could control in manually with a tap of the new inside garage controller mounted to the wall, or using one of the remote garage controllers, or using the outside keypad installed beside my garage. But those are only the low-tech options.

Chamberlain’s smart garage also includes a wall controller and an outdoor keypad.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

With the MyQ app, garage management expanded in all-new directions. The app let me control the garage door remotely from anywhere and receive alerts about it opening and closing. I could also set timers so the garage closes after a certain period, from a few minutes to an hour or two, so I could open the garage for quick tasks and didn’t have to worry about it getting closed. Most of the features extend to other smart home platforms like Google and Alexa, too.

You can even set schedules so the garage opens and closes at a certain time. Maybe that could save users a little time in the morning when getting ready for work, or otherwise match unique schedules and daily needs.

The MyQ app is packed with garage settings.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

MyQ connectivity also lets users set one-time access options for Amazon Key-In deliveries so delivery people can store shipments in the garage for safekeeping, a helpful option to prevent porch pirates in the holiday season. I didn’t get any Amazon deliveries during my testing, but I’ll try this feature out and let you know how it goes when I can.

LED lights dazzle my garage space

Chamberlain’s LEDs are very bright, so don’t worry about garage lighting.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Chamberlain’s Premier smart garage has several model options, including versions with one LED light and those with two. My test model had two LED lights, and I was grateful because they proved sufficient to light up the entire garage by themselves.

These lights are rated at 2,000 lumens, which equals very bright in a space as small as a garage — bright enough that it’s tough to take a picture of them with normal camera settings. If you’re looking for a smart garage that can also take the place of all your old overhead garage lighting, this is the model for you.

You can’t adjust brightness, but you can change many other light settings.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

The light, like the door, comes with multiple settings. I could turn motion detection on or off, depending on whether I wanted the light to pop on every time someone went into the garage. I could also set how long the light stayed on after, up to several minutes, before it automatically shut off again.

If you prefer manual light controls, there’s a separate button on the wall controller to turn on the light separately. It will also automatically turn on whenever you open or close the garage door. There are no brightness settings to dim this light, so you’ll need to get used to the new radiant lighting and hopefully it won’t reveal too many dirty garage corners.

A Secure View AI camera for a garage security boost

This smart garage has a built-in security cam that does a little of everything.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

The smart garage and its lighting are only part of the story. This installation also includes a built-in security camera that folds down from the motor to monitor your garage, or at least part of it.

I’ve tested dozens of security cameras, and this model is high-quality. While I couldn’t narrow down an exact resolution, the field of view is 130 degrees and the camera can pick up plenty of detail no matter which angle you point it.

The camera also includes motion detection and a night vision mode with settings to choose if and when it’s activated. You can livestream footage on the app or set detection features to get alerts.

You can head into live views for the camera, or view recorded footage with a subscription.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

I have mixed feelings about a security camera in the garage. On one hand, it was handy to have eyes on both my car and the garage door, and receive notifications if anything was unexpectedly disturbing them. If you’re worried about garage security – and it’s one of the places that burglars check first for easy entry – a cam like this can bring peace of mind. You can also select AI detection features to specifically notice humans, animals, packages and vehicles when they appear. My tests of these features found them all to be accurate.

This Chamberlain camera has plenty of AI detection to enable.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

However, garages get used very frequently, and I’m a little uneasy about having a camera constantly watching and updating on every little thing. It’s not great for home privacy, especially when it comes to the face detection option, a feature that’s led to multiple 2026 lawsuits against video doorbell companies using facial recognition on strangers.

MyQ’s subscription also unlocks the more controversial face detection feature.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Chamberlain has several settings to mitigate these concerns, and I found them particularly useful. You can angle the camera so it focuses on the garage door and leaves the front portion of the garage unwatched, which is helpful if people are always coming and going. You can also set motion zones so the camera only picks up activity in specific spots.

The camera can record events, but you can choose to record all events or only those related to the garage door, or not record at all. Likewise, you can turn the different types of AI recognition on or off, or shut down the camera altogether if you don’t want to use it. This flexibility made me much more comfortable with the cam.

Options to set motion zones or turn any feature off completely make this camera quite adaptable.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

A final caveat: More advanced features, such as AI detection, motion alerts and cloud video recording/storage, will require a MyQ subscription, which start at $50 per year, around $4 per month. Access alerts are hard to give up, but otherwise I don’t think users need a subscription. However, if you intend to use the smart garage as a cornerstone of your home security, I suggest at least the basic subscription to enhance the camera. There is a free trial, so you can try out the extended capabilities before you decide.

Final thoughts on the Chamberlain Premier Smart Garage Door Opener with Camera

Chamberlain’s smart garage is one of the most complete smart home devices I’ve tried, packing smart access control, scheduling, and camera monitoring with AI detection into one product. It all works very well, too, although you’ll need a subscription for more advanced features.

Being able to automate your garage, manage access codes and control it from afar brings plenty peace of mind, and if you’re worried about garage break-ins and vehicle theft, the camera is a valuable add-on. The bright LEDs can also take the place of most garage lighting.

I also appreciated the many settings in the MyQ app which allowed me to adjust timers and sensors, or turn off features I didn’t want to use, making the entire experience very customizable.

Smart garages this advanced aren’t cheap, and you’ll have to pay several hundred dollars to reinvent your garage. I also highly recommend arranging a professional installation to handle the setup details. The result is a garage dragged happily into the modern age, equipped with better, smoother controls that I appreciated more every day of my testing.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: Will Chinese AI companies slow down? A top House Democrat wants answers
snippet: Image: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images As President Donald Trump prepares to meet tech and AI CEOs in Washington, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) is calling for a treaty between the US and China to keep AI from wreaking havoc on the world. But wrangling leaders in both countries to take action could be a long shot. In letters shared exclusively with The Verge, Khanna - the top Democrat on the House Select Committee on China and a possible presidential contender - asked a US intelligence agency and Chinese AI companies whether they would be prepared for an incident like OpenAI agents' hack of Hugging Face this summer. The companies included DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI, all of which … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
As President Donald Trump prepares to meet tech and AI CEOs in Washington, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) is calling for a treaty between the US and China to keep AI from wreaking havoc on the world. But wrangling leaders in both countries to take action could be a long shot.

In letters shared exclusively with The Verge, Khanna — the top Democrat on the House Select Committee on China and a possible presidential contender — asked a US intelligence agency and Chinese AI companies whether they would be prepared for an incident like OpenAI agents’ hack of Hugging Face this summer. The companies included DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI, all of which are pursuing high-level artificial intelligence.

American and Chinese interests “could not be more different on many issues,” Khanna writes in the letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, “but on this discrete concern, it benefits neither country for humanity to lose control of our destiny.”

“[I]t benefits neither country for humanity to lose control of our destiny”

Khanna requests the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) assess how effectively the US might respond to an AI lab losing control of its bots — a scenario that’s become increasingly common in recent months. Alongside it, he asked the agency to evaluate the Chinese government’s approach to assessing catastrophic AI risks. The information, he says, will help Congress and eventually the White House craft an agreement with their Chinese counterparts.

The letters to DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI ask for documentation about their efforts to achieve “superintelligence” and recursive self-improvement (RSI) — a milestone where AI systems can improve on themselves. He asks about any efforts to implement safeguards and “kill switches” for the technology, as well as whether the companies would commit to inspections by a non-governmental agency if a treaty were struck. The companies and ODNI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Verge.

Khanna’s move follows a meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump at the White House last week. Both men, he says, fail to recognize the risk and urgency around AI. “I think it was constructive that Trump and Xi Jinping at least agreed to talk about AI and have ongoing dialogue about it, but it is not nearly adequate,” Khanna told The Verge in an interview on Monday.

He is also skeptical of a planned Tuesday meeting between the White House, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA), and several American tech executives. “I think it’s an effort to reassure the American people that these tech companies are going to be responsible, and it’s a branding exercise,” Khanna says. “But why should we trust companies that have a motive to maximize profits to be making the rules for what is safe? It’s not that they’re bad people, but would you trust the pharmaceutical executives to determine the rules for what drugs are safe?”

“Why should we trust companies that have a motive to maximize profits to be making the rules for what is safe?”

Khanna ultimately seeks a US-China treaty banning RSI and monitoring frontier AI labs, but he recognizes that’s unlikely to happen anytime soon. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) has similarly called for an AI treaty between the countries, though Republicans like House China Committee Chair John Moolenaar (R-MI) have been skeptical the Chinese government would keep its end of the bargain. In the meantime, Khanna says he’d like a working group with experts from both countries to suggest safety recommendations and methods for ensuring compliance.

But Trump and his allies have been resistant to most regulations or agreements. The morning of his meeting with Xi last week, Trump posted on Truth Social, “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also.” Johnson said on Fox Business that he expected the conversation to revolve around striking “the right balance” of oversight without stifling innovation, warning against losing the AI race against China. Leading US AI companies, however, have called for the US to coordinate with China to slow down the pace of development

In the letter to the Chinese AI companies, Khanna acknowledges they’re unlikely to respond in full. He said they didn’t respond to requests in an earlier letter asking for a commitment to slow down AI development alongside OpenAI and Anthropic. Khanna tells The Verge his goal is to “shame them” and “spark a debate” among Chinese AI companies about safety. While he’s critical of US AI firms too, he says, “at least they’re engaging in safety conversations.”

Khanna remains confident the US will drive AI safety standards, in part because he believes many Chinese models are distilled from US models. And while world leaders may not recognize the threat, they’re “out of touch with the scientists and technologists in their own countries,” he says. “We need to get the technologists and the engineers who understand this really driving the debate, not CEOs who have a vested interest in making profits, and not politicians who lack a technical expertise and who are more concerned about power.”

Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

Lauren Feiner

title: Trump Administration Makes Way for Less Efficient Cars as Fuel Prices Soar
snippet: The Treasury Department’s new fuel economy rule promises $1,300 off the average new vehicle, but will that matter if fuel prices continue to climb?
fullText:
The US Department of Transportation released its new Freedom Means Affordable Cars rule on Monday, resetting the nation’s corporate average fuel economy standards to pre-Biden-Buttigieg-era levels. Secretary Sean P. Duffy called it the end of an “illegal mandate” that forced automakers to build EVs that Americans don’t want, but the new rule, which makes it easier for automakers to build less efficient vehicles against the backdrop of soaring fuel prices, feels more than a touch tone-deaf.

According to AAA, Americans are starting off this week paying an average of $4.48 per gallon for regular and $6.45 per gallon for diesel, with high prices driven largely by the conflict in Iran and instability stemming from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. That’s more than a 50% price increase at the pump since the start of the conflict seven months ago. As part of my recent research on the future of electric cars in the US, I learned that Americans have spent $43 billion more for gas during the war, according to estimates released by the US Senate’s Joint Economic Committee this summer, with no relief in sight.

“With Americans struggling to afford gasoline that is more than $4 a gallon, the Trump administration is going to force them to pay more at the pump,” Kathy Harris, director for clean vehicles at Natural Resources Defense Council, said in a prepared statement reacting to the news. “Oil companies will get a windfall from gutting the fuel economy standards, but the rest of us are going to be handing over more of our hard-earned paychecks to fill up the tank.”

			

More from CNET

The US DOT announced sweeping changes on Monday, resetting fleet fuel economy standards to pre-Biden levels.US Department of Transportation

What’s in the rule

The DOT says its new rule, formally known as SAFE Vehicles Rule III, will cut the average new-vehicle price by $1,300, save people $138 billion over five years, and prevent 300,000 serious injuries and 1,900 deaths by encouraging new-car sales.

The rule sets more relaxed standards for model years 2022 through 2031. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimates that the new standards will still result in a fleet average of 34.9 mpg by 2031, which is up from 2024’s 30.1 mpg, but woefully short of the approximately 50.4 mpg minimum fuel economy for passenger vehicles and light trucks set during the Biden administration. 

In an email to CNET, representatives of the Natural Resources Defense Council point out that the 34.9 mpg target is already “below what automakers on average have already achieved,” which, to me, paints the new rule less as a slow climb and more as simply maintaining the status quo.

Starting with model year 2030, the new rule will also change how vehicles are classified, a move the DOT hopes will discourage automakers from making design changes and adding equipment to small crossovers to tip them into the light-truck classification, with its lighter efficiency standards. In its release, the department says that it hopes this will “[flip] the current fleet mix of approximately 70% light trucks and 30% passenger vehicles to around 70% passenger cars and 30% light trucks” and encourage the return of hatchbacks, wagons and smaller vehicles.

The rule also ends the CAFE credit trading program starting in 2028, eliminating the ability for automakers that exceed federal fuel efficiency standards to earn compliance credits, which they can bank, transfer between their own car and light-truck fleets, or sell to other manufacturers. Closing this loophole eliminates a major cash-flow source for Tesla, which has generated roughly $2.76 billion annually by selling these excess regulatory credits.

Not a win for American drivers

Here’s the thing: The Freedom Means Affordable Cars initiative doesn’t actually oblige automakers to build cheaper cars. Yes, it loosens the targets that automakers are required to hit, not what they choose to sell. That’s not necessarily a win for US buyers.

One possible outcome of efficiency targets relaxing is that the more efficient models that would have arrived to meet the previous, tougher standards get shelved or never greenlit, while automakers choose to build less efficient vehicles, which are often less expensive to manufacture. If fuel costs continue to rise, which depends heavily on when oil flows resume through the Strait of Hormuz, buyers could be left between the rock of high operating costs and the hard place of fewer efficient options. A lower sticker price would be a small comfort if the vehicle costs more to run over the next decade.

The new rule also closes the CAFE credit trading program, closing a major source of cash for automakers like Tesla.

Tesla

Experts have reached out to CNET to share their disappointment. 

“Today, the Trump administration dealt perhaps its greatest blow to affordability and common sense: gutting federal fuel economy standards in the midst of skyrocketing gasoline prices and an impending energy crisis,” Daniel Greene, senior director of Consumer Protection & Product Safety with the National Consumers League, said in an emailed statement. “Nearly two years of sustained assaults on domestic clean energy and unprecedented weakening of energy efficiency standards have helped get us into this mess. Doubling down on failed policies that inflict pain at the pump and exacerbate the affordability crisis will not get us out.”

On paper, I’m on board with the reclassification rules: Making a vehicle less efficient by adding unnecessary off-road and hauling equipment that will likely never be used should not be rewarded with looser efficiency standards. And I like the idea of encouraging the return of sedans and hatchbacks. In reality, though, automakers and Americans are so deeply invested in building and driving SUVs that I don’t know how much reclassification will move the needle. I also don’t hate the closing of the carbon credit trading program; automakers not being able to buy their way out of complying with emissions standards isn’t the worst outcome.

Overall, the experts I’ve spoken with agree that the Freedom Means Affordable Cars rule is a step backward. The administration is pushing a policy that, at best, maintains a disappointing status quo and, at worst, could (and likely will) result in drivers paying more at the pump for fewer choices on the lot.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Antuan Goodwin
						

						

							Senior Writer, Electrified Cars						
					

											

								

											Antuan has nearly 20 years of expertise and experience testing hundreds of cars, including electric, hybrid, plug-in hybrid, hydrogen, and traditional combustion vehicles.

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Every few months, I sit down to look back at the Mac threat landscape, and every time I expect to write about something new. This time I can’t. But that doesn’t mean nothing is happening. In fact, the opposite.

Since I published the Security Bite Q1 2026 review, we’ve seen ClickFix go from the new kid on the block and the technique to watch to now the default delivery method for almost every new Mac stealer. Threat actors are getting much better at using it too (I suppose the kids would call this “locked in”). Recently we’ve seen attackers implement persistence, backdoors, and even infrastructure that hides inside Apple’s own services.

Here’s what you should know as a security practitioner or a malware-fearing Mac owner…

ClickFix is an on-ramp for everything right now

To no one’s surprise, Apple’s 26.4 Terminal prompts didn’t slow this attack vector down.

Nearly every new Mac malware family from the past few months arrived the same way: a fake CAPTCHA or “fix” page that gets the victim to paste a command into Terminal themselves. ClickLock, discovered by Group-IB. A new Go-based stealer Huntress spotted in August. The latest MacSync variant, which Kaspersky found spreading through pages posing as Homebrew and a disk space cleanup tool. More on each soon.

What makes ClickFix so successful is that it doesn’t need to go up against Gatekeeper, notarization, XProtect, or any of the Mac’s incredibly capable antivirus tools. This is really because the user is coerced into infecting themselves by running the script. Apple’s warning prompts were a good first step, but attackers are scrappy and will always find ways around. Like Script Editor.

Stealers are evolving into something much worse

So, ClickFix is the delivery technique. Now let’s talk about the payload.

In its old school form, a Mac infostealer was very much a smash and grab. It would run once, dump your passwords and crypto wallets to something like a Telegram bot, and then vanish. That’s certainly not the case anymore. Just this year, we’ve seen examples like ClickLock that social engineer users into giving up their system password and leave a backdoor behind for round two.

ClickLock stealer malware presenting fake alert to get the user’s system password. 

Doesn’t go away until the user enters the correct one (it verifies).

MacSync, which came into the world as an AMOS lookalike, picked up a backdoor module too. Moonlock Lab put it best in its mid-year report, saying the 2026 model isn’t a stealer, it’s a persistent implant that happens to start with stealing.

Arguably, the more interesting change is how they’re hiding now.

MacSync’s latest version actually pulls its commands from a public iCloud calendar, so anyone watching network traffic just sees the Mac talking to Apple. CrashStealer, found by Jamf Threat Labs in July, posed as Apple’s own crash reporting framework inside a notarized app, so Gatekeeper just let it right through. Neither is a flaw in macOS. It’s attackers figuring out that the easiest way past Mac’s built-in defense mechanisms is to look like something trusted from Apple.

Good explanation of the iCloud calendar trick:

MacSync's iCloud Calendar trick is pretty cool. One MacSync downloader analyzed by Securelist contains a URL such as: https://caldav.icloud[.]com/published/…

It retrieves a public .ics calendar, creates an anonymous pipe, launches zsh -s, sets the pipe as stdin, and feeds the… pic.twitter.com/TTVHfpj07O

— Stephan Berger (@malmoeb) September 27, 2026

What you can do as a user or practitioner

There’s not much users can do beyond updating to the latest versions of the operating system. As of today, that means iOS 27 or 26.7 and macOS Golden Gate or Tahoe 26.7. I would also recommend turning off Screen Sharing if you don’t use it. And the big one: NEVER paste a command into Terminal given to you by a website or pop up alert.

Tibit if you’re defending a Mac fleet: the single most valuable stealer detection right now is Terminal, Script Editor, or osascript spawning from a browser. Pair it with alerts for curl or base64 piped directly into a shell because the first stage doesn’t go to disk. If you’re only scanning files, it’s too late.

title: Qualcomm announces Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 for AI ‘hearables,’ even ones with cameras
snippet: Qualcomm announced the Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 as a substantial chipset for upcoming audio devices, with a massive focus on better AI performance for audio wearables. more…
fullText:
Qualcomm announced the Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 as a substantial chipset for upcoming audio devices, with a massive focus on better AI performance for audio wearables.

The Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 SoC is purpose-built for audio wearables, or “hearables” as Qualcomm puts it in its press release. With the push beyond simple audio performance, the chipmaker is taking the opportunity to build on what audio chipsets can do, as far as contextual image recognition for any camera-equipped earbuds the new chipset might be used in.

As for pure performance, Qualcomm notes the new Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 will be capable of up to 2x greater on-device AI performance. That comes at a lower power consumption rate by up to 40%. Translated to real-world use, the SoC is poised for AI wearables with local and online models that should require less frequent charges. Android XR devices would be a key example, since Gemini will need to live locally and gather information from real-world surroundings.

	

The chipset is also capable of Wi-Fi 6E, so OEMs can position devices to offer on-board or cloud-based AI access.

	

Qualcomm hasn’t abandoned the core principles of the audio chipsets. The Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 will have aptX and XPAN connectivity for better audio quality and Bluetooth range. But it will also leverage AI performance for better ANC built on Qualcomm’s 5th-generation protocol.

The chipmaker goes on to list a few theoretical devices the new SoC would be able to power. Some examples are traditional earbuds and headphones, as well as “open-ear hybrid audio designs, camera-enabled devices, audio glasses, and future multimodal wearables.”

Qualcomm doesn’t mention any key upcoming devices the Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 SoC chipset would live in, but with Android XR devices and more coming from large companies, it likely won’t be long before the new silicon is undergoing real-world use.

title: Did Anthropic Really Make a Big Biology Breakthrough? We Asked Scientists to Weigh In
snippet: Claude’s enzyme discovery is neat, but it’s unclear what comes next, or whether it was truly original.
fullText:
Anthropic’s Claude made headlines last week by discovering an enzyme system that humans had never seen before. That doesn’t happen every day, and Anthropic is quite proud of the work its AI did in finding it. The question is, is Anthropic’s discovery all hype, or could this really be the next big thing in biological research?

The system in question is a CRISPR-like enzyme that was discovered while Claude was scouring through about 200,000 reverse transcriptase samples. This same level of research would’ve taken humans months to conduct, and so Claude is being heralded for doing it a lot faster and actually finding a result worth studying.

Anthropic says human involvement was limited to the prompts and lab work while 950 AI agents scoured through publicly available databases to identify something unique. It took about 21 hours to spot the enzyme, and then it was confirmed by human scientists to be a novel enzyme, meaning that it had never been observed by science before. 

			

More from CNET

“This is an exciting example of how AI agents can contribute to biological discovery,” Feng Zhang, professor at MIT and the Broad Institute, said in a statement. “The identification of RNA-repeat arrays associated with reverse transcriptases is genuinely intriguing and merits further investigation.”

What is CRISPR?

There are a lot of big words here, so let’s pause to decipher some of them. CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) is a defense system found in bacteria. This defense system is used to fight off viral infections. That’s right, bacteria can get sick too. 

The way it works is that when a bacterium survives a viral infection, it copies a snippet of that virus’s DNA into its own DNA, and that library of snippets builds up over generations. When a virus attacks the bacterium, the bacterium summons an RNA with the appropriate viral snippet. The RNA uses that snippet like a paint-by-numbers to guide a cutting protein that cuts the viral DNA in just the right places so that it can’t replicate, thereby killing the infection. CRISPR is this entire process from start to finish. 

Researchers discovered CRISPR in 1987 and eventually figured out that they could use that system in gene therapies, thereby removing harmful or mutated DNA in living organisms using a similar method as CRISPR and replacing it with clean, nonmutated DNA. It took darn near 40 years, but the first CRISPR medicine was approved in 2023 in the UK, and then in 2024 by the US Food and Drug Administration. 

And what is a reverse transcriptase?

The other glossary term you need to know is reverse transcriptase. This is an enzyme in some organisms that uses RNA as a template to build DNA. This is the reverse of how things normally go, where DNA is used as a template to build RNA, and so it has its own name and classification. 

It’s a defining characteristic of many viruses, including HIV. Learning that HIV uses a reverse transcriptase enzyme to replicate helped scientists devise some of the first medicines to treat it, and the information is still used today in modern therapies that have contributed to HIV no longer being a death sentence. 

However, unlike CRISPR, reverse transcriptases are in all kinds of other organisms aside from viruses. 

So what exactly did Anthropic find?

One of the things about CRISPR is that it contains many repeating DNA fragments, a primary indicator that helped scientists identify it in the first place. In the decades since, scientists have only ever found CRISPR in bacteria and archaea, single-celled organisms separate from bacteria and other microbes. 

This is notable because this is basically what Anthropic found with its army of Claude bots. 

“What Claude noticed is another type of protein, a reverse transcriptase, sitting next to a long array of repeating DNA, which is very similar to how CRISPR is laid out,” a representative for Profluent, an AI lab that made OpenCRISPR-1, the first AI-generated gene editor, told CNET in an email. “This particular reverse transcriptase had been seen before. The array next to it and a partner protein alongside it are what Anthropic is sharing.”

The enzyme was found in a bacteriophage, which is a virus that specifically attacks bacteria. Viruses with large DNA genomes like this are commonly known as jumbo phages. Anthropic named this previously uncharacterized system “array-associated reverse transcriptases,” or ART for short. 

How big of a deal is this discovery?

This is the real conversation. CRISPR is one of the biggest scientific discoveries in modern history, and its ability to rewrite DNA has a ton of potentially viable uses in medical science. So, finding something like CRISPR, as Anthropic did, is definitely going to warrant some discussion.

The problem is twofold. One, it took scientists about 20 years to figure out how CRISPR even worked, and then nearly another two decades to build the first medicine with it. That means it could take a while before we find out if this discovery is important or not. 

“Scientists are finding interesting sequence patterns all the time, relatively speaking,” Bonnie Berger, head of the Computation and Biology group at MIT’s Computer Science and AI Lab, told CNET in an email. “The bottleneck is then figuring out the purpose and function of these systems using deeper analysis, expert biological knowledge, and complementary targeted experiments.”

Gene editing technology has led to new medical treatments, like therapies for sickle cell disease, developed in labs like the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute’s Cellular and Molecular Therapeutics Laboratory, at the National Institute of Health in Bethesda, Maryland, seen here.Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

Anthropic has no illusions when it comes to this side of things.

“Our work to understand the primary function of ARTs is ongoing,” Anthropic said in a statement. “However, we think it is important to share such findings early, both to demonstrate Claude’s capabilities and to give the broader community insight into what we’re working on.”

The other problem is that another group of scientists may have already found this particular enzyme. Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a computational biologist at the University of Copenhagen, told The New York Times over the weekend that his team found this enzyme back in 2022. 

“They are the same systems we have been studying for years,” Mestre told the NYT. He points to a patent that contains the research, for which he is listed as a co-inventor. 

Anthropic says that it was unaware of this research.

So, is this a win or not?

One thing that the greater scientific community has been able to agree on is that the speed at which this enzyme was found is actually pretty awesome. Anthropic said that it could have taken human researchers weeks or months to find this needle in the proverbial haystack. All the experts CNET spoke to agreed with this assessment. 

“We have hardly scratched the surface of exploring the biological systems represented in species sequenced outside of a handful of model organisms,” Berger said. “So, many accomplished scientists could spend their careers studying interesting sequence patterns without getting to this one.”

It’s no secret that AI has racked up a laundry list of failures over the years. It’s a terrible lawyer, an even worse friend and its contributions to social media are commonly referred to as slop. 

The same is not true in this case. Anthropic using Claude to find ART in 21 hours is far faster than any human would’ve done it without an overabundance of luck. If Anthropic and its peers can repeat this success over and over, AI may be adding an item to the very short list of things it’s actually good at doing. However, Berger does warn that lazy AI research can lead to “an overwhelming volume of low-impact observational findings that smothers important, targeted research on promising disease treatments.”

Mestre and his team are less convinced, however, stating that they can’t say for certain whether Claude found these novel enzymes on its own or if the bot had been trained on the treasure trove of unpublished research the scientists had been uploading to Claude for years up to this point to assist them in their own research. That research would’ve sent Claude to that enzyme like a homing beacon.

“I mean, coincidences happen,” Mestre told the Times. Even so, Mestre and his team are shutting down their projects with Claude and moving to other models, just in case. The pickings are slim, since OpenAI was accused of doing this same thing while solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Problem, and could not rule out that the model had been trained on “deidentified data derived” from Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster, the mathematicians who actually solved it.

So, all told, Anthropic will have to wait a while longer to collect its Nobel Prize in biology, cure every disease on Earth or even score a clean win for Claude without accusations hanging in the air.

title: Adobe expands creative tool access to Google Gemini, brings Acrobat to Claude
snippet: Adobe today announced two major expansions to its AI chatbot integrations, bringing its creative tools to Google Gemini while adding Acrobat tools to Claude. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Adobe today announced two major expansions to its AI chatbot integrations, bringing its creative tools to Google Gemini while adding Acrobat tools to Claude. Here are the details.

Adobe expands tools to Gemini, adds Acrobat to Claude

For the past year or so, Adobe has been working to bring its creative tools to AI chatbots and other productivity tools, such as ChatGPT, Slack, and Copilot.

Today, the company is announcing two expansions to that effort.

First, Adobe is expanding its integration with Claude. The company already offered access to creative tools from Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, InDesign, Adobe Express, Adobe Stock, and more. Today, it is also adding Acrobat tools to the same plugin across Claude and Claude Code on desktop, the web, and mobile.

Adobe says users can get started as a guest, or sign in with their Adobe account “to unlock the full plugin experience, including higher usage limits, additional tools and continuity across sessions.”

Here’s how Adobe describes some of the new capabilities:

Work with Acrobat tools in Claude: The Adobe plugin now includes popular Acrobat tools for working with PDFs. Organize PDFs by deleting, combining or splitting pages; redact sensitive information; and convert or export PDFs to other file formats.

Edit and analyze PDFs directly: When you want more hands-on control, open your PDF in the new interactive editor to reorder pages, edit text or mark up the document with comments and highlights. You can also invoke the new Document Review skill and ask Claude to analyze your document and add recommendations and notations directly in the editor.

Refine designs with Express: Building on the conversational editing already available in Claude, you can now go further with a layer-based interactive editor for Express designs, giving you hands-on control over individual elements of the design. Select and customize images, copy, colors and fonts independently, so you can refine exactly what you want without needing to regenerate the entire design-all within your Claude workflow.

The second piece of news today comes for Google Gemini users across all plans. Starting today, Adobe is bringing tools from Photoshop, Lightroom, Adobe Express, and Firefly directly into Gemini.

This means that users can ask Gemini to enhance photos, create marketing assets, and customize designs using Adobe’s tools without leaving the conversation.

To get started, navigate to Personal Intelligence, select Adobe under Connected Apps, and sign in with your Adobe account or create one for free if you don’t already have one.

Adobe adds that users only need to describe what they want, and Adobe “orchestrates the right tools and steps to get you there.”

		
		

Some of the things Adobe says users can now do in Google Gemini include:

Create consistent, polished product photos: Upload your product photos and describe the look you’re after. Adobe can help optimize lighting and color, crop images consistently and prepare a polished collection that’s ready for your storefront, website or marketing materials.

Turn one design into content for your social channels: Ask Adobe to create social-ready versions while preserving your branding and messaging, making it easier to adapt and publish content wherever your audience spends time.

Customize professionally designed templates for your marketing needs: Describe your campaign, target audience and the style you’re looking for, and Adobe will surface Express designs that best match your needs. From there, you can ask Adobe to personalize the text, imagery and colors to quickly create polished marketing materials.

title: HomeKit Weekly: ULTRALOQ releases its first UWB smart lock that works with Apple Home
snippet: Hands-free smart lock unlocks/entry has always been a bit ahead, marketing-wise, compared to what the technology offers. Location-based auto-unlocks work until they fail for no specific reason, and using a key seems much easier. ULTRALOQ’s new Bolt Mission takes a different approach than most smart locks as its using ultra-wideband to detect when you are approaching the door, vs just tracking your location via GPS. more…
fullText:
Hands-free smart lock unlocks/entry has always been a bit ahead, marketing-wise, compared to what the technology offers. Location-based auto-unlocks work until they fail for no specific reason, and using a key seems much easier. ULTRALOQ’s new Bolt Mission takes a different approach than most smart locks as its using ultra-wideband to detect when you are approaching the door, vs just tracking your location via GPS.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

UWB vs Bluetooth

The Bolt Mission combines Bluetooth Low Energy discovery, UWB, and built-in radar-based presence sensing to figure out whether you’re actually approaching the door from outside or inside your home. That last part is what separates it from Bluetooth-based auto-unlock. The lock isn’t just tracking “Is an authorized iPhone near me?” It’s actually analyzing precise distance and direction of approach and making a local decision based on said data. The intent detection logic runs between your iPhone and the lock without requiring a cloud connection or a hub inside your home.

The end result is that you keep your iPhone in your pocket as the Xthings Home app runs in the background, and the door unlocks as you walk up to it. iPhone users who have used UWB features in AirTags will recognize how much more accurate this kind of spatial awareness is vs Bluetooth.

The rest of the new collection

On top of the Mission lock, ULTRALOQ is also launching the Bolt Pro and Latch 5 Pro alongside the Bolt Mission, and those two are worth looking at separately from the Bolt Mission. Both are Aliro-Certified, which means tap-to-unlock through Apple Wallet or Samsung Wallet. Aliro is the open standard developed by the Connectivity Standards Alliance, the same organization behind Matter, with support from Apple, Google, and Samsung. It’s tap-to-unlock from your wallet, but it’s not the same as Apple Home Key, which is Apple’s unique NFC implementation. Both are good, but they’re just different

If Home Key is on your requirements list, you’ll have to look elsewhere. If you want a tap-to-unlock option that works across platforms or you prefer the Aliro standard, the Bolt Pro is a deadbolt, and the Latch 5 Pro covers lever-style doors like side entrances, garage-entry doors, and home offices. Both support fingerprint, PIN, app control, and physical key backup alongside the digital wallet option. I have an older Bolt in my office, and I love the fingerprint unlock.

All three locks are Matter-certified and work with Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and more.

Wrap up on ULTRALOQ Bolt Mission

The ULTRALOQ Bolt Mission is the lock I’m most curious to check out in this new collection. UWB-based detection is a ne  approach to hands-free unlocking, and if it works as described, it’ll fix the core problem that has made auto-unlock not 100% reliable for me. The Aliro-based Bolt Pro and Latch 5 Pro are solid additions to the lineup for anyone who wants tap-to-unlock across platforms, but just go in knowing they’re not using Home Key. 

You can buy the ULTRALOQ Bolt Mission and the rest of the new collection from Amazon or directly from ULTRALOQ.

title: As Android XR nears, smart glasses are only getting more popular despite Meta backlash
snippet: There’s been a near-constant stream of backlash against Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses in recent months, but that hasn’t stopped people from buying them, as a new report reveals that shipments have grown by over 250%. more…
fullText:
There’s been a near-constant stream of backlash against Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses in recent months, but that hasn’t stopped people from buying them, as a new report reveals that shipments have grown by over 250%.

Counterpoint Research reports that, in the first half of 2026, shipments of AI smart glasses have risen by 263% year-over-year. Meta holds 94% of the market with its Ray-Ban and self-branded glasses models, with Xiaomi and Alibaba each holding 1% in second and third place, respectively. 

Display-less glasses make up 96% of all shipments, with brands such as Rokid, Meta, Even Realities, and others splitting the remaining 4% of shipments for glasses that have a built-in display, but that segment is up nearly 450% year-over-year. Notably, no figures have been shared on just how many glasses units are being shipped/sold.

North America is the biggest market for display-less smart glasses, taking up 50% of the global market share, while China is a slightly bigger market for glasses with a display. 

	

Meanwhile, competition is brewing as Samsung & Google prepare to launch the first Android XR-powered smart glasses. The initial release will be display-less, focusing on integrations with Android and Gemini for interactions through your smartphone, Wear OS watch, and audio to accomplish tasks and interact with the glasses.

title: Source: Inference provider Modal Labs closing in on $750M round at $15.75B valuation
snippet: The new financing is expected to more than triples the AI infrastructure startup's valuation from just four months ago.
fullText:
AI inference infrastructure provider Modal Labs is nearing a $750 million funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation that includes the investment, according to a source with knowledge of the funding. The size of the round has not been previously reported, though Axios and Bloomberg have reported other details of the deal.

The new round would more than triple Modal’s valuation from the $4.65 billion it reached when it announced its $355 million previous fundraise just four months ago.

Modal Labs declined to comment.

The deal comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open-source models. Other inference startups are also in talks to raise fresh capital at much higher valuations. Baseten is nearing an infusion of capital at a $26 billion valuation, doubling what it was worth in June, Bloomberg reported. Meanwhile, Fireworks and Fal, a startup providing inference for video and image generation, have also talked to investors about new rounds that would significantly increase their valuations, according to The Information.

Although revenue for these companies has been growing rapidly, their margins are thin, largely because the cost of acquiring or leasing compute remains very high. Fireworks announced in July that its annualized revenue had hit $1 billion, a fivefold increase from the year before. Multiple inference-focused startups are expected to reach the same revenue milestone by year’s end, according to our source.

Modal was founded in 2021 by CEO Erik Bernhardsson and CTO Akshat Bubna. Bernhardsson, who is Swedish, spent more than 15 years building data teams at companies including Spotify, where he helped build the music-streaming service’s recommendation system, and Better.com, the online mortgage lender, where he served as chief technology officer. Bubna studied math and computer science at MIT and was an early staff engineer at Scale AI, the data-labeling startup, before co-founding Modal.

The company, which is based in New York and estimated to have roughly 150 employees, lets developers train AI models and run other compute-heavy workloads without managing their own servers. Its web page lists customers that include the coding startup Cognition, the AI music generator Suno, the fintech company Ramp, and the publishing platform Substack. 

As of May, Modal had surpassed $300 million in annualized revenue, it told Reuters at the time.

The fundraising talks come two months after Modal was pulled into one of the AI industry’s most closely watched security incidents. In late July, Modal disclosed that a customer’s data had been compromised as part of the same hacking campaign carried out by a rogue OpenAI agent against Hugging Face.

Modal Chief Technology Officer Akshat Bubna said the breach traced back to a flaw in a customer’s own code, not to Modal’s systems. “We’re aware a Modal customer published an unauthenticated endpoint that allowed anyone on the internet to use their sandboxes for code execution,” Bubna said in a statement to press outlets at the time. “This was used by the rogue agent. Modal’s platform was not compromised in any way,” he’d added.

Marina Temkin is a venture capital and startups reporter at TechCrunch. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she wrote about VC for PitchBook and Venture Capital Journal. Earlier in her career, Marina was a financial analyst and earned a CFA charterholder designation.

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

The SSO tax might be the most backward pricing model in enterprise software. Single sign-on should be required for sign-up, yet SaaS vendors routinely lock it behind their most expensive tiers. It should be the opposite. You should have to pay more not to have SSO. The result is entirely predictable: companies skip it, weak passwords fill the gap, and hackers thank everyone involved. I think there’s a real opportunity here for Apple, and it starts with an acquisition.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

The SSO tax is a security problem with a pricing name

I covered this in my recent article on Dashlane’s Vault Enforcement: on average, 37% of enterprise SaaS apps are not managed via SSO, leaving a critical security gap, especially given that adoption of password management is still low, all things considered. That’s a third of the average company’s app surface protected by nothing more than a username and password. Some of that is legacy passwords and setup complexity, but a meaningful chunk is vendors charging a premium for the login method that actually keeps organizations safe. When SSO costs 2x or 3x as much as the base plan, SMB will often skip it

Everyone in the industry agrees this is broken. Nobody with enough leverage has been motivated to break it. Identity providers charge per user, SaaS vendors charge for integration, and the customer pays more for something that should be required. Imagine if MFA costs extra?

Clever already solved this for K-12

Here’s the thing: this problem has already been solved once, just not in the enterprise. Clever is the SSO and rostering platform used by a vast majority of K-12 schools. I’ve been a Clever admin multiple times in my career, and I absolutely love the service. Side note: Their support is among the best in the industry. I recently called them, and it felt like I was talking to someone up the road from me who knew exactly what my problem was and how to solve it. Seriously, shout-out to the Clever support team and to Clever leadership, who invest in it.

The model is the interesting part. Clever is free for schools and districts. Application vendors pay to be on the platform because the Clever app gallery is how they reach customers. That flips the SSO tax completely. Instead of the customer paying extra for secure login, the vendor pays for access to the customer, and secure login is simply how the platform works. Districts came to demand Clever support as part of any purchase, and vendors fell in line because losing deals was more expensive than integrating with Clever. I will not purchase a K-12 tool that doesn’t support Clever. 

Clever was acquired by Kahoot in 2021 and has continued to operate as its own platform since. 

Why Apple should buy it

Apple already has the pieces around the edges. Managed Apple Accounts, Apple Business, Apple School Manager, Platform SSO in macOS, and Sign in with Apple all exist today. What Apple doesn’t have is the connective service: a true identity layer that sits between organizations and the thousands of SaaS apps they use, with an economic model that makes SSO free for the customer.

Buying Clever gets Apple three things at once. First, a proven platform and team that has already executed this exact playbook at a massive scale in K-12. Second, an instant dominant position in K-12 identity, a market where Apple continues fighting for device share against Chromebooks, and where owning the login layer would make Apple hardware even stickier (Google owns this today with Google Workspace). Third, and most interesting to me, a model it can extend upmarket: Apple-backed SSO that’s free for businesses, funded by vendor-side participation, and deeply integrated into macOS and iOS

Imagine “works with Apple SSO” becoming a requirement in enterprise buying models, the way Clever support became one in district purchasing. Customers demand it in the deal, vendors integrate because they have to for a deal, and the SSO tax is then rendered dead. You can take this even further with deep integration on the procurement side with direct ordering through Apple.

Wrap up

The SSO tax persists because no one with leverage has been motivated to kill it. Apple has the cash. Apple is in a dominant spot in the enterprise at the moment, and killing the SSO tax would be a clear way to drive enterprise services revenue, but not from the customer directly.

title: Apple releases macOS 27.0.1 Golden Gate, plus macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 [U]
snippet: Following two release candidates, Apple today released macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1, as well as macOS 27.0.1. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following two release candidates, Apple today released macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1, as well as macOS 27.0.1. Here are the details.

macOS 27.0.1, macOS 26.7.1 and macOS 15.8.1 now available

After two release candidates, Apple is now rolling out macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1, in addition to macOS 27.0.1 Golden Gate, the first update since the release of macOS 27 earlier this month.

Today’s releases come exactly one week after Apple rolled out the second round of release candidates, which also included public releases the following day.

Apple’s release notes during the RC mentioned only standard security fixes and performance improvements, but recent point releases have included significant security patches, many of which address vulnerabilities discovered with the help of AI tools.

Apple has even confirmed that the growing capabilities of AI tools are affecting its security release cadence. In June, the company said it had pushed out fixes originally planned for version 26.6 ahead of schedule because AI can speed up the development of malicious hacking tools, reducing the amount of time Apple wants to leave between making fixes public and getting them into users’ hands.

Apple will likely release the security details for macOS 27.0.1 Golden Gate, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 in the coming hours, and we’ll report back with the noteworthy tidbits.

Update, 1:59 p.m. ET: Apple says macOS 27.0.1 Golden Gate “has no published CVE entries,” but says macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 fix the following issue:

CoreGraphics

Available for: macOS Sequoia

Impact: Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution. Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.

Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved bounds checking.

CVE-2026-86950: Meta Product Security

The release build for today’s macOS releases are:

macOS Sequoia 15.8: 24H32

macOS Tahoe 26.7.1: 25G241

macOS 27.0.1 Golden Gate: 26A5434

title: Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Sonnet 5.5 model, details here
snippet: Anthropic is upgrading Claude Sonnet, replacing Sonnet 5 from June with Sonnet 5.5 as the best medium-sized model. more…
fullText:
Anthropic is upgrading Claude Sonnet, replacing Sonnet 5 from June with Sonnet 5.5 as the best medium-sized model.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 upgrades Anthropic’s medium model

Anthropic currently offers a few AI models under the Claude umbrella. 

The three main models are Haiku (smallest and cheapest), Sonnet (medium size and price), and Opus (largest and most expensive of the three).

There’s also Fable/Mythos, which is even more capable and costly, which represents Anthropic’s highest tier.

Today’s new Claude model follows the arrival of Opus 5.5 last week. Anthropic promised to upgrade Sonnet and Haiku “in the coming weeks” at the time.

Introducing Claude Sonnet 5.5, the second model in the Claude 5.5 family.

It’s a clear upgrade over Sonnet 5, runs more than 30% faster, and costs up to 30% less for most work. pic.twitter.com/UvXD8mDTF1

— Claude (@claudeai) September 28, 2026

Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 is strongest at everyday tasks with a clear scope, including fixing bugs and creating polished documents, slides, and spreadsheets.

The company also highlights its design capabilities, from refining user interfaces to producing slides that follow templates and need minimal editing.

Early testers described it as a better collaborator than Sonnet 5, Anthropic says, with clearer writing and speed suited to quick iteration on less complex tasks.

Sonnet 5.5 keeps Sonnet 5’s pricing: $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens, and $0.20 per million cache reads.

Anthropic says it typically uses far fewer tokens to complete the same work, while generating output more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5, making it the fastest Sonnet model to date.

With cybersecurity capabilities comparable to Opus 5, Sonnet 5.5 is the first Sonnet model to launch with cyber safeguards and fallbacks similar to those used for Anthropic’s most capable models.

Its biology safeguards remain unchanged from Sonnet 5. Anthropic says both target a narrow set of high-risk requests, leaving routine software development and most life sciences work unaffected.

title: Samsung rolling out Android 17, One UI 9 for more Galaxy S26 users – here’s everything new
snippet: After a lengthy delay, Samsung is finally rolling out its Android 17-based One UI 9 update for Galaxy S26 users in the US more broadly. more…
fullText:
After a lengthy delay, Samsung is finally rolling out its Android 17-based One UI 9 update for Galaxy S26 users in the US more broadly.

Samsung announced its One UI 9 rollout early this month, but updates didn’t start flowing. Last week the update finally started to trickle out in the US, but only for users on T-Mobile. 

Now, the floodgates are starting to crack. 

Galaxy S26 users on unlocked devices in the US are now seeing One UI 9 land, Android 17 in tow, at least for those who were enrolled in the beta program. It’s still not a full rollout, but it’s another step towards the full debut. SammyGuru and others spotted the rollout which, for those in the beta, measures around 650MB, while Android Authority also cites some Samsung changelogs that detail everything new.

	

Samsung’s official changelog follows (edited for formatting):

One UI 9

Galaxy AI

Enhanced Now nudge

Now nudge provides helpful suggestions in more places throughout your Galaxy experience. In addition to the keyboard, suggestions will now appear in conversation notifications and in a floating button in the bottom right corner of the screen. There are also several new types of suggestions, like entering reservation details or addresses and saving places in Google Maps.

Focus on someone important

My FanCam lets you select a person in a video and follow them automatically while cropping out the rest of the video.

Interpreter keeps your conversation in front of you

In conversation mode, you can scroll through the whole conversation while you’re still talking.

See useful information during calls

See relevant events and other information related to your current call on the call screen.

Productivity and multitasking

More customizable quick panel

You can now rearrange and customize the controls in your quick panel even more than before. You can change the size of the brightness and volume sliders as well as the media player. You can also separate the sound mode button from the volume slider.

Privacy, security, and device protection

Warranty and care

The new Warranty and care menu in settings lets you check your warranty information and access diagnostic checks and useful information for keeping your Galaxy in top condition.

Lock down your phone quickly

It’s now easier to securely lock your phone in a hurry. Just press and hold the Volume down and Side buttons at the same time or tap the Power button in the quick panel. This prevents biometrics from being used the next time you unlock your phone.

Location access transparency

Stay on top of your location privacy. A blue indicator will appear at the top of the screen when an app accesses your location. Tap the indicator in the quick panel to see which app it is.

Stronger security and privacy protection

Alerts will appear in your Now brief to let you know about risks from malware, apps from unknown sources, unnecessary permissions, and other issues that may put your security and privacy at risk. Apps that have been identified as malicious or vulnerable will be blocked from opening until you make a decision about whether to remove them.

AI privacy alerts

Get help protecting your personal data. AI will monitor how apps use permissions and notify you about unnecessary access to your personal data.

Samsung Health

New look for Samsung Health

Samsung Health has been redesigned to make your health data easier to understand. Enjoy clearer visuals, improved charts, and a more engaging experience to help you reach your health goals.

Customize your Health home screen

Resize cards and organize them by category, like Activity, Sleep, Mindfulness, and Nutrition, so your top priorities are easy to access.

Log health data quickly

It’s now easier to add your health information right from the Samsung Health home screen. You can log your mood, meals, and more. You can even use the camera for faster input.

Advanced trend analysis

Track your progress with improved trend charts in Samsung Health. View data in hourly, daily, or weekly intervals, pinch to zoom in for a closer look, and overlay multiple charts to compare your performance across different periods.

Monitor changes in your sleep vitals

Samsung Health helps you notice meaningful changes in your sleep health data. Use Galaxy Watch or Ring measurements to better understand your daily health patterns.

Manage your heart health

Track key health metrics and lifestyle factors that affect your heart. A daily score based on your sleep, exercise, BMI, and blood pressure helps you better understand your current heart health trends.

Track your cardio load

See how your workouts and activity impact your heart so you’ll know when to push harder and when to rest. Your target cardio load range adjusts daily based on your recent activity and training focus.

Check your fitness index

Your Fitness Index is an overall score calculated using five key fitness metrics: body composition, cardio, strength, flexibility, and endurance. Set a goal and unlock personalized insights tailored to your results.

Keep your ears safe

The new Hearing tracker monitors sound levels detected by your Galaxy Watch and headphone audio levels to help you manage your exposure to loud sounds.

View your cycle and body rhythm

Get a more personalized view of your cycle and body rhythm with new cycle tracking options. You can view your cycle information in your calendar and better understand your health patterns.

Bixby

Activate Bixby with a gesture

Talk to Bixby just by raising your phone close to your mouth and speaking. No wake-up word needed.

Manage your conversations

Keep your chats organized. Search them, rename them, or pin your favorites. You can also delete all of your past conversations at once.

Bixby on the Home screen

Add a Bixby widget to type or talk to Bixby or jump directly to your conversation history.

Accessibility

Discover new Accessibility features

Check the What’s new menu in Accessibility settings to learn about and try the latest Accessibility features for your Galaxy.

Text spotlight for easier reading

Need a closer look? Tap any text on the screen to show it enlarged and highlighted in its own window. You can also customize the font size, colors, and other settings to match your preferences.

Physical keyboard shortcuts

Use shortcuts on your physical keyboard to access the Accessibility settings you need without touching the screen.

Mouse keys enhancements

New options are available when using your keyboard for mouse interactions including speed and acceleration control. You can also use the keyboard’s number pad to point and click.

Replace swipe with single tap

The Replace swipe with single tap option is now located in the Dexterity and interaction menu instead of the Assistant menu for easier access.

Select to speak

Get quick audio readouts without turning on full TalkBack. With the new Select to speak feature, you can select an item on your screen, like text or an image, and hear it read or described out loud.

Improved TalkBack updates

TalkBack updates can now be applied with a simple app update from the Play Store, helping you get the latest accessibility features and enhancements.

Even more improvements

New Lock screen clock

The default clock on your Lock screen has been redesigned with a cleaner and more modern look that adapts to match your wallpaper.

Samsung DeX enhancements

It’s easier to move an app window from one desktop to another using the menu at the top of the window. Desktop previews are now available at the top of the Recents screen, making it easier to switch with a single tap.

title: Meta is launching ‘VR Glasses’ next year for $1,300
snippet: Alongside its new audio-only and Ray-Ban smart glasses, Meta today also unveiled new “VR Glasses” which take the experience of a Quest into a far slimmer form factor with an external processing puck. more…
fullText:
Alongside its new audio-only and Ray-Ban smart glasses, Meta today also unveiled new “VR Glasses” which take the experience of a Quest into a far slimmer form factor with an external processing puck.

Arriving in “Spring 2027,” Meta VR Glasses are a second attempt at a high-end VR experience from Meta following the failure of its Quest Pro headset. And this is definitely a more refined and focused effort.

Meta VR Glasses aren’t a headset directly, rather going for a far more compact form factor that puts 5K displays in front of your face and offloads all of the processing and battery components off to a puck. The glasses themselves weigh merely 100g, around 1/5 that of the Meta Quest 3 headset. 

The actual form factor is similar to XREAL’s upcoming Android XR-powered Aura glasses.

	

Meta VR Glasses support Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, as well as IMAX Enhanced content – Disney+ will support VR through expanded aspect ratio starting in November. ESPN will also be bringing 8K streaming starting with college football, and more will be coming through NBC Sports, the MLB, and more in the future. 

Controllers are not needed, Meta says, with hand gestures for general use and even the ability to put a virtual keyboard on the desk in front of you. 

It’s all powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset and Meta says to expect around 3 hours of battery life from the puck for media playback, with 45W fast charging to top it back off. 

Meta VR Glasses will be available next year at a price of $1,299.

Meta launches audio-only glasses and Gen 3 Ray-Ban with slimmer designs

Meta Ray-Ban update will block the most obvious loophole for disabling the privacy LED

title: Google Messages rolls out new swipe for timestamps & reply gesture
snippet: Following the long-press menu, Google Messages is widely rolling out new ways to access timestamps and direct replies. more…
fullText:
Following the long-press menu, Google Messages is widely rolling out new ways to access timestamps and direct replies.

Previously, you could tap on a message bubble to see the sent time, read receipts, and RCS lock icon. Meanwhile, swiping left would let you send a direct reply.

A redesign today changes all that. To see timestamps, you can now swipe left anywhere in a conversation. This also shows the RCS encryption status. Being able to see all times instead of having to tap the bubbles individually is an improvement.

	

To reply to a message, you now have to swipe right on the bubble. Some amount of precision is required. You can still tap the message to see the read receipts.

	

As of today, the most widely rolled out design appears to be the old two-circle look instead of the single version that has been in testing for ages. In fact, in a real show of inconsistency, the new design widely appears on an individual message’s Details page and might also show up on the homepage.

Google changing the swipe behavior is likely the biggest disruption today. When you tap on a message, Messages will briefly have the timestamps peek out as a hint about the new behavior.

We’re seeing this widely rolled out with version 20260910_03_RC02 of Google Messages.
