title: macOS 27 Top Features: much more than just Siri AI [Video]
snippet: Although Apple’s revamped personal assistant is no doubt the headlining feature in macOS 27 Golden Gate, there are many other new features and refinements in this year’s update that don’t involve Siri AI. Read our post as I cherry-pick a few of my favorite new macOS 27 updates, and be sure to watch our video as I walk through them all. more…
fullText:
Although Apple’s revamped personal assistant is no doubt the headlining feature in macOS 27 Golden Gate, there are many other new features and refinements in this year’s update that don’t involve Siri AI. Read our post as I cherry-pick a few of my favorite new macOS 27 updates, and be sure to watch our video as I walk through them all.

App icon revamp

macOS 27 changes almost all of the built-in app icons in some way, with a few icons like Siri, Preview, and Chess undergoing complete redesigns. Other app icons, like Finder, Photos, and Reminders, also receive noticeable revamps, with a trend toward emphasizing the Liquid Glass design language. Few app icons were spared changes in macOS Golden Gate, but many of the updates are subtle.

If you watch my video below, you’ll see slider comparisons showing how each app icon looked in macOS Tahoe and how it now looks in macOS Golden Gate.

Some of the updates, like the Photos app, I’m a fan of. Other updates, like Finder, I’m not fully sold on. Let me know what you think about the app icon changes down below in the comments.

Video: macOS 27 Top Features and Changes

Subscribe to 9to5Mac on YouTube for more videos

Widespread HDR support

One of the coolest things about macOS 27 is its broad support for HDR across the OS’s visuals. Icons, toolbars, and other parts of the Liquid Glass design language gain support for additional dynamic range that users of HDR-capable displays will immediately notice.

To identify which elements have additional dynamic range, you can use macOS’ built-in Digital Color Meter utility to see where shadows or highlights clip while viewing native SDR values. Be sure to watch my video as I explore various areas of the OS to show HDR support.

Digital Color Meter: Compare the clipped area when viewing SDR vs brighter highlights when using EDR

If you’re a Studio Display XDR user, you’ve no doubt seen the differences, but even if you haven’t ponied up for Apple’s most expensive display, you’ll still be able to enjoy the benefits on a third-party display that supports HDR.

I recently went hands-on with Asus’ ProArt QD-OLED 32-inch 4K display, and, given the panel technology, the HDR effects throughout the OS stood out. Unlike Apple’s first-party displays with Extended Dynamic Range support, you’ll need to venture into Settings > Displays and enable the High Dynamic Range toggle to enjoy the benefits.

Most recently, I’ve started using the Dell UltraSharp U3226Q QD-OLED display, which I’m really enjoying, and I will be posting a review on it soon. On both displays, the HDR elements pop, such as the blinking cursor within the newly redesigned Spotlight/Siri AI interface.

Design updates

macOS Golden Gate features a ton of design updates to address complaints users raised about macOS Tahoe. One of my biggest complaints was the mismatched corner radii between certain windows.

macOS Tahoe’s egregious corner radius issue has been fixed in Golden Gate

Of course, this wasn’t the only complaint addressed, but it was the one that mattered most to me. Other areas that were fixed were the floating side bars, which are now back to being edge-to-edge side bars, toolbars have been revamped with an obvious line of demarcation, and the Liquid Glass effect itself has been improved, including a new slider that lets users have more choice over the amount of transparency vs tint throughout the OS.

Another major complaint from users about macOS Tahoe was the unnecessary clutter heaped onto the menus. In macOS Tahoe, nearly every menu option got its own corresponding glyph, which made the menus look like a mess.

Tahoe vs Golden Gate: Apple learned that not every menu option needs its own glyph

If every menu item has an icon, eventually you’re going to run out of icon options that make sense, while reducing the effectiveness of the glyphs that were there before. I’m so glad that Apple fixed this issue.

iPhone Mirroring

iPhone Mirroring on macOS 27 got three major improvements that make the feature so much better on Golden Gate.

You can now access Control Center from a mirrored iPhone.

You can resize the iPhone mirroring interface to match more closely the iPad mini aspect ratio.

You can play back DRM-protected content from your iPhone on your Mac without a blackout.

Needless to say, iPhone Mirroring just got a lot more useful in macOS 27!

9to5Mac’s Take

Although Siri AI takes up most of the headlines, macOS Golden Gate is not just about Siri. I cherry-picked a few of my favorite new additions in this post, but there are lots more to explore. Watch my full video for a rundown of everything new, and let me know what your favorite new features are in the comments.

title: Apple vs. Adobe: How does iOS 27’s AI photo editing compare to Photoshop?
snippet: I’ve been using Photoshop’s generative AI features to remove unwanted objects and extend photos since Adobe introduced them in 2023. They’ve been hit or miss for me, but they’re certainly a lot faster than the old-fashioned approach of masking, cloning, and manually painting things out. But with iOS 27, Apple has significantly improved its Clean Up tool and introduced the new Extend tool, and I was curious to see how Apple’s offerings compare with Adobe’s. So, with the help of a friend, I put both to the test using a variety of photos to see how they stack up. more…
fullText:
I’ve been using Photoshop’s generative AI features to remove unwanted objects and extend photos since Adobe introduced them in 2023. They’ve been hit or miss for me, but they’re certainly a lot faster than the old-fashioned approach of masking, cloning, and manually painting things out. But with iOS 27, Apple has significantly improved its Clean Up tool and introduced the new Extend tool, and I was curious to see how Apple’s offerings compare with Adobe’s. So, with the help of a friend, I put both to the test using a variety of photos to see how they stack up.

For this article, my friend Jürg was kind enough to provide several photos from his travels throughout Switzerland and Europe. He takes much better photos than I ever could, and takes pictures of more exciting subjects than my corner of Ohio has to offer. You can see more of his photography on Instagram. I narrowed the selection down to six photos: three to test object removal and three to test image extension.

All photos were shot on an iPhone 17 Pro Max and edited on an iPhone 18 Pro Max running iOS 27.0. The Clean Up tool in iOS 27 has three options: Auto, Fast, and High Quality. I left the setting on Auto for all three tests.

Photoshop tests were done on a MacBook Pro running Adobe Photoshop 27.10.0 using the “Firefly Fill & Expand” model. I selected the objects using either the Object Selection Tool or Lasso Tool, then chose Generative Fill and left the prompt box blank.

For the Extend tool, I used whatever extension Photos selected by default. The Extend tool in Photos limits how far you can expand the edges of an image, while Photoshop doesn’t have the same restriction. To keep the comparison as consistent as possible, I used the result from Apple’s Photos as my reference, and had Photoshop create something in a similar size.

I made every effort to keep the HDR appearance as consistent as possible between the photos edited in Photos on iOS 27 and those edited in Photoshop, but there was some minor variation.

Making things disappear

Left: Original photo

Right: iOS 27 Clean Up

First up is the removal of this red chair in front of the yellow door. This was the first photo I tested with the new Clean Up tool, and I have to say, it left quite a positive impression. The result looks very believable, and the only real mistake I noticed is that the rivet behind the chair’s left armrest was also removed instead of being correctly reconstructed. It’s not something I’m convinced most people would notice, though, and it would be an easy fix to clone back in with Photoshop. I was particularly impressed by how the shadow beneath the chair was replaced with a texture that matches the surrounding scene while also maintaining the existing lighting.

Left: Original photo

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Photoshop doesn’t do as good a job as Apple’s Clean Up tool here. The chair’s shadow remains and looks more like an oil stain. The door’s rivets are misaligned, and one is obviously missing. The replacement texture also contains significantly more visual artifacts. Overall, it isn’t nearly as clean or realistic as what Clean Up produced.

Left: Original photo

Right: iOS 27 Clean Up

I was really impressed with Clean Up’s results here. Not only did it remove the plate with bread, but it also added a nice reflection of the mug and jars. Notice it even got the handle of the spoon right in the reflection. A nice detail. Clean Up also completely removed the plate’s shadow from the napkin. I thought removing a red plate from a red table of the same color might prove more of a challenge for Clean Up, but nope! If I had one nitpick, it’s that Clean Up left the crumbs from the plate, though removing them would be very easy to do by running Clean Up again over that area.

Left: Original photo

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Photoshop removed the plate with bread well enough, but again, it had issues with leaving behind an out-of-place shadow. The napkin looks dirty or wet here, but at least Photoshop didn’t leave behind as many pesky crumbs.

Left: Original photo

Right: iOS 27 Clean Up

This photo proved to be a much bigger challenge for Clean Up. After attempting to remove the man on the right, Clean Up left behind a garbled mess with plenty of obvious artifacts. The leaves are too chunky. It struggled in a similar way on the left side of the image, where the woman with white hair was standing behind the white flowers. Clean Up also left behind a “ghost” of the dog’s head, though it arguably blends in with the stone wall and is much more noticeable in this side-by-side comparison.

Left: Original photo

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Photoshop had no issues removing the woman on the left behind the white flowers or the man on the right behind the leaves, realistically filling in both areas in the process. The end result is a very convincing photo that looks like nobody was ever there. Photoshop also avoided leaving behind any phantom shadows this time.

Adding to the picture

Left: iOS 27 Extend

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

I thought this photograph of these old, winding steps would make for a good test because I didn’t think it would be immediately obvious to either AI what it was looking at, and I was curious to see how each would interpret the scene. Or even what it would do with it. It looks like iOS 27’s Extend tool interpreted the photo as something more like a ceiling fan, rounding off the ends of the stairs as though they were blades. Photoshop, on the other hand, simply extended the stairs outward and did a surprisingly good job of matching the wood grain.

Left: iOS 27 Extend

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Extend does an excellent job living up to its name here. It extends the scene really well and creates a very convincing final image. Notice the windows are believably repeated and the bridge on the right side of the photo, while arguably too smooth, still manages to look fairly convincing.

Now look at Photoshop’s attempt. Actually, Photoshop, did you even make an attempt? This is a complete failure by just about every measure. Pure, obvious AI slop. The windows and roofline in the upper-left corner of the photo look terrible. The bridge on the right doesn’t have anything resembling the realistic arch Apple created, and for some reason, Photoshop decided the waterfall should randomly change direction rather than continue along the existing river line.

Left: iOS 27 Extend

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Extend again manages to create a convincing image that, while not perfect, is significantly better than what Photoshop produced. Extend creates a believable table with some books or magazines, and the flowers in the vase look much more realistic than those generated by Photoshop. The decorative ornamentation above the left door also matches the real ones in the photo surprisingly well. There is some strangeness on the right side of the photo, where Extend has added a radiator, a random power cord, and a table for some reason.

Perhaps the biggest difference between Extend and Photoshop is at the ceiling. Extend has recreated more of the wood from the opposite wall, while Photoshop has tried to turn it into something more like a structural beam.

Photoshop, meanwhile, can’t seem to generate an image without the telltale signs of AI slop. Its table has too many legs and appears to simply “break off” before blending into the floor. The ornamentation above the door is less convincing, missing one of the “swirls” and doesn’t have the textured paint found on the real ornamentation in the photo.

I wouldn’t say either is perfect, but when it comes to realism, I think Apple’s solution edges out Adobe’s.

The good, the bad, and the AI slop

It’s worth mentioning that Photoshop requires a subscription to use, but none of the features I tested consume generative AI credits. Adobe does give users the option to choose other AI models that may require credits, but I didn’t use those models in my tests. Apple, too, has made it clear that “usage limits may apply” to some Apple Intelligence features and may charge for expanded access in the future. 

It’s clear that Apple has made significant improvements to the Clean Up tool over previous versions of iOS. I’ve tried it before and always found it underwhelming, but now it’s genuinely good. The new Extend tool is impressive as well, and I found it significantly better than Adobe’s offering in my tests. Adobe gives you unlimited refinements and the ability to adjust results with prompts, but I question the value of those benefits if additional generations and prompts simply churn out more obvious AI slop. Apple may be more limiting in this regard, but its initial results are much better to begin with.

Of course, results will vary depending on the photograph, the complexity of the scene, and what you’re asking the tools to do. These were simply the results I got from the photos I tested.

How about you: Have you had a chance to try out Apple’s new Clean Up and Extend tools? If so, what do you think?

title: Still running iOS 26? Update your iPhones, iPads and Macs for this urgent security fix
snippet: Apple says the bug was used to attack "specific targeted individuals" running iOS 26, which the majority of Apple customers are still using.
fullText:
Apple has fixed a security vulnerability in its iOS 26, iPadOS 26 and macOS 26 operating systems that the company says “may have been exploited” by hackers. The tech giant said the now-fixed bug could be used to launch “an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.”

According to a listing on Apple’s security pages, the bug was found in the main graphics engine that powers the user interface and visuals on iPhones, iPads and Macs. 

Meta’s product security team was credited with the discovery.

Details of the bug, officially classed as CVE-2026-86950, were not released, but a device’s graphics engine typically has broad access to the rest of the device’s operating system. A successful exploit could potentially allow a hacker to steal a broad range of personal data from an affected device.

When reached by TechCrunch, spokespeople for Apple and Meta did not provide comment about how the bug was discovered, or how many people had their devices hacked due to this vulnerability, if any. It’s also unclear who may be exploiting the bug, such as government spyware makers or cybercriminals.

While the bug affects Apple’s previous generation of operating systems, it remains in wide usage. Almost four-in-five of Apple’s iPhone owners are still running iOS 26, according to the company’s own statistics. Devices running the latest version, iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27, released earlier this month, also received a software update on Tuesday, but are unaffected by the bug under attack.

A separate ‘zero-click’ bug now fixed

News of the security patch comes soon after Apple fixed another critical security bug, known as CVE-2026-86869, which could have allowed hackers to silently steal data from affected iPhones, iPads, or Macs. 

Belgian cybersecurity research firm ironPeak published a detailed writeup last week explaining that the bug was a “zero-click” vulnerability that could be invisibly triggered via a maliciously crafted iMessage, without the user’s knowledge. Such bugs require no interaction from the victim, such as clicking a link, and are highly sought-after by surveillance vendors and spyware makers. 

Per ironPeak’s post, the bug is capable of bypassing BlastDoor, a security feature that Apple implemented to prevent malicious code, like spyware, from escaping iMessage’s sandbox and hacking the user’s device.

Apple fixed the bug in September with the release of iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27, and credited ironPeak’s Niels Hofmans with the discovery, alongside security researchers at Meta who confirmed their findings in a post on X.

It’s not yet known if this bug had been used in cyberattacks before it was fixed.

title: Leaked images reveal new colors for Amazon’s next entry-level Kindle
snippet: Amazon typically introduces new Kindle models a few months ahead of the holiday shopping season, and this year it looks like that will include a bigger update to the entry-level Kindle than what debuted in 2024. The last upgrades to the basic Kindle model were limited to a brighter backlight, a new dark mode, and faster page turns, but according to leaked images shared by WinFuture, the next version will come with a minor redesign and expanded color options. The last entry-level Kindle model was available in black and matcha green colors, and while the leaked images don't reveal the official names Amazon has given the new colors, they inclu … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Amazon typically introduces new Kindle models a few months ahead of the holiday shopping season, and this year it looks like that will include a bigger update to the entry-level Kindle than what debuted in 2024. The last upgrades to the basic Kindle model were limited to a brighter backlight, a new dark mode, and faster page turns, but according to leaked images shared by WinFuture, the next version will come with a minor redesign and expanded color options.

The last entry-level Kindle model was available in black and matcha green colors, and while the leaked images don’t reveal the official names Amazon has given the new colors, they include light blue, green, and mauve options, in addition to black.

A more enticing reason for current Kindle owners to upgrade is that the new version of the entry-level model relocates the power button from the bottom of the e-reader to the top right edge, which could help prevent users from accidentally putting it to sleep when resting the e-reader on something while reading. The leaked images also reveal more rounded corners for the new Kindle’s screen and WinFuture speculates, based on some of the images that appear to show the e-reader with a slightly recessed E Ink panel, that multiple versions could be available with different display features.

The leaks don’t reveal anything about other upgrades to the entry-level Kindle including what E Ink screen it will use, how much storage it will come with, battery life, or pricing. The 2024 version of the basic Kindle debuted at $109.99 but last month Amazon increased its price to $149.99 as a result of ““significant increases in memory and storage component costs.”

title: With Dazzle, Marissa Mayer bets your camera roll has more info on your life than your inbox
snippet: The former Yahoo CEO is introducing a new AI personal assistant based entirely on your photos.
fullText:
When former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer earlier this month told me she was finally ready to unveil Dazzle, the personal AI assistant that raised an $8 million seed round last December, I couldn’t help but wonder if she’s playing copycat to Meta’s Muse, Instinct, and the wave of similar tools that have flooded the market over the past month.

But when Mayer finally gave me a demo, Dazzle proved it’s taking a different approach. Instead of building context about you from text-heavy apps like email, calendars and shopping histories, Dazzle’s AI assistant gets all its context from a single source: your camera roll.

“I think that photos are an underappreciated source of information,” Mayer said. “You’ll be surprised what we can learn about you and how good a job we can do with your photos.”

Mayer argues that if a photo is worth a thousand words, your camera roll is worth millions. By analyzing all the photos stored on your phone, Dazzle claims to understand your hobbies, interests, food and style preferences, how you like to spend their time, and with whom.

“We understand whether or not you like to ski, where your most recent trip was, what types of things your kids are into,” Mayer said.

It’s no surprise that Mayer has built an assistant centered around photos. Her previous startup, Sunshine, launched an AI-powered photo-sharing tool called Shine in 2024. While that product was widely criticized for its outdated design, failed to attract widespread usage, and eventually shut down, Mayer says it nevertheless built “interesting IP.”

I was eager to try Dazzle, which users can interact with through its app or via text. Dazzle splits its functionality into two core experiences. For immediate tasks, it can scan recent photos to pull details — like populating your calendar from an event flyer, or finding a repair-person after spotting a broken garage door in your camera roll.

Second, it mines your photo library to come up with personalized ideas for everything from holiday vacations to birthday gifts.

Image Credits:Dazzle

Given that plenty of tools can parse pictures — like looking up where to buy a product, or searching information on an interesting art piece — I was far more curious to test what Dazzle could learn from my photo history.

For instance, Mayer uses Dazzle to brainstorm family outings. By scanning her photos, she says, the assistant deduced that her family loves escape rooms, and subsequently suggested multiple SF Bay Area locations she’d never heard of.

When I tested Dazzle with a request for vacation recommendations, it suggested several Mediterranean spots, likely picking up on my past trips to Spain and Greece. But it also threw in Sicily, which surprised me since I was there four years ago. After some more tinkering, I noticed it has blind spots — it failed to remember my daughter already knows how to roller skate when I asked if I should buy her a pair for her next birthday.

Despite the hiccups, though, I appreciated Dazzle’s ideas for activities, like suggesting a local pottery studio, or a bioluminescent kayak tour in Tomales Bay.

I’m sure the product will improve with time, and while I’m undecided on whether I’ll keep using it, I like that its suggestions feel more personal than what you’d get from an AI assistant that only knows your calendar and email.

In the meantime, Mayer contends that given security concerns with products like Instinct and Muse, users may feel more comfortable handing over their photo libraries to an AI instead of granting it access to sensitive data like emails and messages.

She emphasized that Dazzle prioritizes privacy, and discards any personal information the AI flags as sensitive.

This flurry of new AI assistants is an exciting time for consumers. And while Dazzle isn’t as broadly useful as other offerings quite yet, it offers a glimpse of a future in which AI can do more than just execute tasks; it actually knows who you are.

title: OpenAI says Apple Intelligence users showed little interest in ChatGPT integration
snippet: As reported by The Financial Times, new court filings show that OpenAI was disappointed by the adoption of ChatGPT through Apple Intelligence, which it says “dramatically underperformed” after launching in 2024. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
As reported by The Financial Times, new court filings show that OpenAI was disappointed by the adoption of ChatGPT through Apple Intelligence, which it says “dramatically underperformed” after launching in 2024. Here are the details.

OpenAI asks court to rule before trial

In August 2025, Elon Musk said that X, now part of SpaceXAI, would sue Apple and OpenAI over alleged collusion to shut out competitors in the AI space, stemming from OpenAI’s deal with Apple to make ChatGPT part of Apple Intelligence and Siri.

When the lawsuit was filed, it actually went beyond Musk’s original public complaint about App Store rankings. X and SpaceXAI also accused Apple of trying to stifle the development of “super apps,” including X’s effort to turn itself into an “everything app.”

In the weeks and months that followed, all companies involved filed briefs, accusations, and defenses with the court. Apple and OpenAI have argued, among other things, that their deal was not exclusive as the complaint alleged, while court filings have also revealed new details about how the partnership worked behind the scenes.

One of those details surfaced today in a filing from OpenAI. As first reported by The Financial Times, OpenAI “said it was disappointed by how little interest Apple generated from iPhone users after the two companies struck a deal in 2024 for ChatGPT to power ‘Apple Intelligence’.”

From the report:

When the 2024 deal was agreed, OpenAI expected a “halo effect” from promotion and brand association with Apple, as well as more subscriptions coming from Apple Intelligence users, Wednesday’s court document says.

But a month after the ChatGPT integration launched, it “appeared to be off to a slow start” and OpenAI was cutting its forecasts for how many weekly active users it expected to attract, it said. By the summer of 2025, “it was clear that Apple’s integration of ChatGPT was dramatically underperforming”.

The report notes that today’s filing contains multiple redacted conversations, but the unredacted portions show that OpenAI executives were concerned Apple could “want to move faster” to secure another AI partner.

When Apple Intelligence was first announced in 2024, Craig Federighi said in an interview that Apple ultimately wanted users to be able to choose between different AI models, specifically pointing to Google Gemini as a potential future integration.

That specific partnership never materialized, but Apple has since turned to Google’s Gemini models to help power the new Siri AI, while Xcode has expanded to support coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI.

	

Back to today’s filing, The Financial Times notes that it also points to the way Apple implemented ChatGPT as one possible reason for the slow adoption, as the integration was turned off by default.

Finally, as noted by Reuters, OpenAI is also arguing that recent securities disclosures from SpaceX undermine SpaceXAI’s claims that the Apple partnership harmed competition. In its filing, OpenAI said SpaceX’s IPO registration statement was “replete with disclosures diametrically opposed” to the competitive harm alleged in the lawsuit.

For these reasons, OpenAI is asking Judge Mark Pittman to rule in its favor before trial on SpaceXAI’s antitrust claims. The case is currently set to go to trial in January.

title: Ex-Tesla team raises $12.5M to put supply chains on autopilot
snippet: Atomic's agentic supply chain software is now being used by companies like DoorDash and HelloFresh.
fullText:
Supply chain startup Atomic came out of stealth last year with founders who promised to use their experience at Tesla to streamline inventory and boost customers’ bottom lines.

At its core, Atomic decides how much inventory a company should have and where by simulating scenarios, then recommending, or even automatically choosing, a response. The approach traces back to a crisis. Atomic’s founders built an early version of this system during the 2018 Model 3 production ramp at Tesla, when the automaker’s own spreadsheets couldn’t keep up with how quickly planning needed to change.

In the year-plus since Atomic co-founders Michael Rossiter and Neal Suidan started talking publicly about their work, that shift has become real for customers — including big tech companies like DoorDash and HelloFresh. It has paid off financially, too. Atomic’s annual recurring revenue has quintupled since the beginning of this year, according to Jon McNeill, a former Tesla president and the founder of DVx Ventures, where Atomic was incubated.

That growth just helped Boston-based Atomic lock down a $12.5 million Series A funding round, bringing its total funding to just north of $15 million to date. The new round was led by growth equity firm Klass Capital and Seattle VC stalwart Madrona Venture Group. Atomic has also brought on longtime Tesla planning director Jeff Goodrich as its CTO and third co-founder.

“If you think about running a supply chain, running an operating model, it’s like an infinite search space for optimization that you’re trying to figure out all the decisions you could make at any given time — and then it changes all the time too,” Rossiter, who is Atomic’s CEO, said in an exclusive interview with TechCrunch. “AI can play the role of finding all of the best paths through that forest.”

“The company has transitioned from pilot customers into real customers, and by real customers, it’s DoorDash-scale customers,” said McNeill, who’s also on Atomic’s board, in an interview. “The product has evolved from being an optimization platform that gives recommendations to a platform that not only gives recommendations but it makes decisions, so it’s fully autonomous in that sense, and so DoorDash is running, I think, 90% of its purchasing across hundreds of sites.”

For food-focused customers like DoorDash, for instance, Atomic’s software helps cut down on waste and spoilage. And each new industry Atomic works in presents different challenges, Rossiter said.

“The cool thing about Atomic is it’s a general model of how you think about supply chains and operating models, and so no matter what that system looks like, our AI can can adapt to it and tailor fit it,” he said. “We’re working with CPG [consumer packaged goods], we’re going deep with mobility and manufacturing clients right now as well, and working that space, kind of going back to our Tesla roots.” 

Making the agentic software useful and adaptable for multiple industries was a big part of what drew investor interest for the Series A, Rossiter said. But it was also Atomic’s ability to deploy quickly with new customers.

“We gave them this challenge from a board level of compressing their onboarding time and really making it a non-event for a customer to turn this on,” McNeill said. Suidan, who is also Atomic’s chief product officer, ran point on that challenge, McNeill said. He was able to push Atomic’s agentic AI to the point it was able to figure out the “decision rules” that a customer’s staff might have, even if they hadn’t been  written down anywhere.

“Then customers were saying, ‘Okay, then you might as well make the decision and free my time up,’” McNeill said. “And where executives, I think, kind of got it was — decision speed is an advantage in any business. And this was one of our first principles at Tesla. When I got to know Elon, he said the thing that will separate us from all of our competitors is decision speed, because decision speed compounds. Like, I make a decision today, I build on that decision tomorrow, et cetera, and it takes one of our competitors, like Ford or Toyota, 30 days to make the first decision.”

Rossiter said he’s excited to help pull customers’ supply chain efforts out of spreadsheets and into advanced software that can help make planning decisions. It’s an evolution he’s seen CFOs lead for their own organizations, but he said it’s rarer to find someone doing the same for operations.

“Finance data always gets the priority. Operating data doesn’t always get that,” he said.

title: Protego Ventures closes debut $125 million fund for Israeli defense tech
snippet: Protego Ventures, the first and largest dedicated defense tech VC in Israel, just completed its final $125 million closing, TechCrunch learned exclusively.
fullText:
Defense and venture capital used to rarely overlap, but that’s no longer the case. Defense tech VC dealmaking set a record in Q1 2026, and new VC firms have emerged around the world to invest solely in defense startups.

One of these is two-year-old Protego Ventures, which presents itself as the first and largest dedicated defense tech VC in Israel. Led notably by two women, Lital Leshem and Lee Moser, it has just completed the final close of its debut fund with $125 million in capital commitments, TechCrunch learned exclusively.

This fund size is enabling Protego to invest between $5 million and $15 million per company, with a focus on startups “addressing the critical defense and security needs of Israel and the global community,” according to its website.

These include the likes of drone maker XTEND, its first portfolio company, which went public on the NYSE earlier this month. That’s also why Protego stopped short of its $150 million target: a smaller fund magnifies the impact of a single big win on overall returns, and with XTEND now looking like a potential “fund maker” — a single investment capable of returning the whole fund — raising more capital would only dilute that upside among a larger pool of investors. “Nobody wants to share the pie,” Leshem said.

Ares Management is one of Protego’s biggest backers. The investment firm suggested that Leshem and Moser join forces and start Protego in the aftermath of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel, with the conviction that new technologies would be key to boosting Israel’s defense capabilities in the face of new threats, Leshem said.

With a $30 million investment as a limited partner, Ares gave Protego the support it needed to start investing right away, Leshem said. Besides XTEND, its portfolio also includes startups such as ASIO, which develops situational awareness systems and has partnered with Anduril.

Leshem says the reception in defense circles has been strong. “On the military side, there is a lot of respect, and people are coming — even under the radar — to talk to us, to learn from us, to train with us, and for sure get our technology and innovation.”

Still, the Israeli market is easier to navigate for insiders, and Protego’s two founders are leaning into their networks. Moser, a seasoned venture capitalist, will remain a managing partner at the generalist VC firm AnD Ventures. As for Leshem, who co-founded a startup that was acquired for $625 million in 2025, she also brings 11 years of experience in the military and intelligence field to their approach.

“Everything changed on October 7,” Leshem told TechCrunch. She was deployed, while pregnant, as a reservist on the day of the attacks. “And basically until the delivery room, I was there, witnessing and getting the first-row seat to how the battlefield acted differently from what I knew in the past decade.”

Protego won’t have the field to itself for long. Israeli authorities have taken notice of the same shift, awarding VC firms Adir Capital and Sling Capital about $33 million in state guarantees to invest in military and dual-use technologies, with other funds also raising capital for similar bets. (Leshem said Protego was too far along in its own fundraising to take part in the government’s tender.) 

Protego, meanwhile, is already planning its next move: a second fund in the first quarter of 2027, backed by Israeli institutional investors and one large U.S. commitment Leshem has already secured, with a broader scope that includes early-growth American defense-tech companies.

title: Gemini app starts rolling out big side panel simplification, settings redesign
snippet: The next big update to the Gemini app on Android and iOS is beginning to roll out with a focus on simplifying core navigation. more…
fullText:
The next big update to the Gemini app on Android and iOS is beginning to roll out with a focus on simplifying core navigation.

There are no major changes to the homepage, with the first differences found in the side panel. Search has moved to the top-right corner, while the chat history now offers filters: All, Ready, Needs attention, and In progress.

“Scheduled” is a new item in the list and replaces the “Scheduled actions” page. You get “Suggested” prompts like Create a news digest or Build a study quiz.

“Customize” is the big update today. The “Discover” tab surfaces skills, which are replacing Gems, and third-party connected apps. Notably, skills are activated using the ‘@’ symbol instead of a forward slash like in Gemini Spark. This page feels like a mini-app store for Gemini.

	

Meanwhile, the “Connectors” tab serves as a modernized “Connected Apps” page. Gemini is leaning into that app store parlance with the ability to “Uninstall” from the overflow menu.

Meanwhile, Gemini is getting a much-needed Settings redesign when you tap your profile avatar in the top-right corner or the gear icon. Manage account and Usage limits make up the first grouping, followed by:

Preferences: Notifications, Personal Intelligence, Avatar, Gem manager, Theme, Voice, Media, Device controls, Gemini Notebook

Data & privacy: Import memory, Contact info from your devices, Gemini Apps Activity, Your public links, Privacy Help Hub

Support: Help, Report a problem, About, Updates 

This redesign is not yet widely rolled out and only appearing on one of our Google Accounts. That said, it’s appearing on both Android and iOS.

title: Google says Chromebook updates end in 2034, ‘many’ models move to Googlebook OS
snippet: As Googlebook arrives, Google is offering a bit more information on what Chromebook owners can expect going forward. more…
fullText:
As Googlebook arrives, Google is offering a bit more information on what Chromebook owners can expect going forward.

Google has said that Chromebook updates will continue in the Googlebook era, while some models will also be eligible for upgrades. On a support page, Google provides a bit more detail.

Starting with Chromebook updates, Google says that “Chromebooks you have today will continue to receive updates through their supported lifetime,” with all Enterprise and Education management capabilities remaining in place as well:

We will maintain support for current Chromebook devices running ChromeOS as outlined in our Auto Update policy and the Chromebooks you have today will continue to receive updates through their supported lifetime. Chromebooks remain available for all school and enterprise deployments today.

Your active ChromeOS Enterprise Upgrade and ChromeOS Education Upgrade associated with existing devices will remain and maintain their current management capabilities.

Google adds that similar management tools will be coming to Googlebook, but they’re not available yet. Apparently they’re planned for the second half of 2027. Meanwhile, Google says that “many” existing Chromebook models will be eligible to transition from ChromeOS to Googlebook OS. More details are coming “soon.” A later note specifies that Google is referring to “newer commercial Chromebook models.”

	

Many of our newest Chromebook devices will be eligible to transition over to Googlebook OS. Details on migration paths and device eligibility will be shared soon.

We are working to deliver a comprehensive management experience for Googlebooks which will start rolling out in the second half of 2027.

Notably, Google specifies a year when ChromeOS updates will come to an end in a later note – 2034. Chromebooks with a 10-year update policy that extends past 2034 will be eligible to move to Googlebook OS.

ChromeOS devices will continue to receive regular updates and security patches through mid-2034. For qualifying devices purchased today whose 10-year support lifecycle extends beyond 2034, Google is committed to supporting your transition to Googlebook OS, with many devices offering direct migration paths.

This 2034 date was previously mentioned in a court case as the time when Google would “phase out” ChromeOS.

	

Finally, in regards to apps, Google says that it is “committed” to web developers despite an increased focus on Android apps on Googlebooks.

Googlebook pre-orders are open now, with models shipping in early October.

title: Google is killing off Gemini’s Gems in favor of ‘skills’
snippet: As all-in-one AI agents like Meta's Muse and Instinct take off, Google is opting to end a feature that built task-specific agents.
fullText:
As all-in-one AI agents like Meta’s Muse and Instinct take off, Google announced it’s shutting down the Gemini feature known as “Gems,” which had allowed users to build custom AI assistants for specific tasks. However, the work users invested in creating the Gems won’t be destroyed. Gems will be automatically migrated to “skills” that can be used across different AI tasks.

Details about the change are being shared in the Gemini app, where a message warns users that Gems will become skills starting on November 17, 2026. The company said it will migrate the Gems to the new format, so users won’t have to do anything to make the transition. The Gems themselves will remain usable until then.

Launched in 2024, Gems were meant to help users teach their AI to perform certain tasks without having to repeat the instructions. For instance, some of Google’s premade Gems had included a learning coach, a brainstorming assistant, a career guide, a coding partner, and an editor. Users could also make Gems for their own needs, like a running coach, nutritionist, or vacation planner. These custom assistants could also be shared with others, which Google had hoped would help make its Gemini AI app more popular.

Image Credits:Google

The news of Gems’ shutdown is another example of why Google shouldn’t be so quick to give every new AI feature its own brand name, icon, and prominent placement in its app’s navigation — especially if it’s going to shuffle things around over time, merging one feature into another. (To be clear, this has been a failing point of Google’s strategy long before the AI era. At one point, for instance, the company was operating multiple different messaging and communication apps at the same time.)

Yet, even as skills, the former Gems still aren’t as consumer-friendly as just typing in text to a chatbot like Meta’s Muse. Instead, Google notes you’ll have to enter a forward slash “/” in a task thread to select the skill you want to use — a user interface that engineers, not regular folks, tend to prefer.

Gems’ wind-down was first reported over the weekend by 9to5Google.

title: Apple Maps just added two new features in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 is packed with a wide array of new features for iPhone, including in Apple Maps. Here are the two tentpole iOS 27 features for Apple Maps, plus some miscellaneous improvements. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is packed with a wide array of new features for iPhone, including in Apple Maps. Here are the two tentpole iOS 27 features for Apple Maps, plus some miscellaneous improvements.

Apple Maps in iOS 27 gets upgraded Flyover feature and Local Lists, plus other improvements

Apple Maps doesn’t look drastically different when you open it in iOS 27. But Apple has a variety of big and small improvements in its latest update.

One tentpole feature is an upgraded Flyover experience. Per Apple:

Apple Maps brings an enhanced Flyover experience, which combines aerial imagery with AI to enable users to view imagery in stunning detail for select cities around the world like never before. Whether scouting a location before a trip or simply exploring a city from a new perspective, the enhanced experience gives users a sharper and more lifelike glimpse into destinations across the globe.

Apple also highlights a new Local Lists feature that’s available in the US:

With Local Lists, Apple Maps users in the U.S. can find the perfect spot for meeting friends, dining, and more. Using intelligent insights from what’s trending, Maps surfaces locally relevant collections of places — from trending restaurants to great spots to take kids — so it’s easy for users to find what they are looking for. All insights are derived with privacy in mind and never tied to individual users.

Beyond these two tentpole changes, iOS 27 also has a variety of other improvements:

More Suggested Places: The new Suggested Places feature that arrived in iOS 26.5 now lets you swipe horizontally through many more suggestions, so it’s not limited to just two placed

Trending Restaurants: The search screen now shows a Trending Restaurants section

Natural language search for routing: AI search expands to routing specifics

Maps Parked Car widget in Smart Stack: Makes it easy to find your car via Apple Watch

Offline Maps update improvements: Apple doesn’t say what the exact improvements are

iOS 27 also brings certain features to more territories around the world, including Visited Places and Guides. And the Maps icon has been refreshed with a new design, as seen above.

snippet: Apple has just released iOS 27.0.1, a new iPhone software update with key bug fixes for issues introduced in iOS 27. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Apple has just released iOS 27.0.1, a new iPhone software update with key bug fixes for issues introduced in iOS 27. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27.0.1 fixes iPhone 18 Pro Face ID issue, plus includes additional bug fixes

iPhone users, Apple has just launched its latest software update. iOS 27.0.1 is now available to install via Settings ⇾ General ⇾ Software Update.

Here’s what Apple’s official release notes say:

This update provides bug fixes for your iPhone, including fixes for the following issues:

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max may unexpectedly restart when Face ID fails to authenticate

A color artifact may appear on photos captured at 2x under certain lighting conditions at f/1.48 on a small number of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max devices

Opening Notification Center and Control Center simultaneously may cause the touchscreen to become unresponsive

As 9to5Mac previously reported, some iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max users experienced crashes when Face ID was unable to properly authenticate them. Apple promised a fix was coming this week, and now it has delivered via iOS 27.0.1.

Out of the listed fixes in Apple’s release notes, only the Notification Center and Control Center issue applies to all iPhone models. 

	

But Apple’s notes aren’t typically comprehensive of all changes, so older iPhones will likely benefit from other, unmentioned bug fixes in iOS 27.0.1 too.

iOS 27 launched two weeks ago as a major new iPhone software update. As happens most years around this time, the public release brought some bugs to the surface that Apple wasn’t able to discover during beta testing, so iOS 27.0.1 fixes some of those issues.

An update is available for iPad users today too: iPadOS 27.0.1. The release notes for iPadOS simply say: “This update provides bug fixes for your iPad.”

title: Instagram partner schools can now post content only their students can view
snippet: Meta last year launched a school partnership program for Instagram, in which it promised to prioritize student reports of cyberbullying. The company has now expanded the program to allow schools to post stories and notes that only their own students can view – alongside support for clubs, teams, and more … more…
fullText:
Meta last year launched a school partnership program for Instagram, in which it promised to prioritize student reports of cyberbullying.

The company has now expanded the program to allow schools to post stories and notes that only their own students can view – alongside support for clubs, teams, and more …

Instagram School Partnership Program

Instagram is a platform that doesn’t exactly have the best of track records when it comes to teenage mental health. Even the company’s own internal research showed that Instagram could be harmful to as many as 20% of teenage girls using the apps by increasing anxieties about physical attractiveness and popularity, among other things.

Cyberbullying has been another significant problem for teen users of social networks, and Meta last year launched a program intended to help schools tackle the issue. When schools signed up to its partnership program, Meta promised that reports filed by students and staff would be prioritized.

Reports submitted by school partners that may violate Instagram’s Community Standards will be prioritized for review. Schools will also receive status updates on the reports and notifications as soon as Instagram takes action on the report.

New school features

Meta says it is today adding a number of new features to the program.

Channels. These allow schools to share updates to parents and students. Only school administrators can post messages in channels.

School Stories and notes. Both staff and students can post these, and they will only be visible by verified students at the school. School administrators can remove posts.

Clubs and Teams. Anyone in the school can create clubs and teams to act as a central hub for communicating relevant events and information.

Student directory. Students can access a directory of other students at their school on the platform. This is visible only to other students and teen followers they follow back.

Meta says that the new features are intended for use outside of classroom hours, noting that teen accounts allow parents to block usage during school hours.

Verification of high school students is carried out by UNiDAYS, the same company Apple uses to allow access to educational pricing.

title: Peak XV ups Surge seed investment ceiling to $5M, unveils 18-startup cohort
snippet: Thirteen of the 18 startups in Peak XV’s latest Surge cohort are targeting global markets, while more than half are based in India.
fullText:
Peak XV Partners, one of the largest venture capital firms investing in markets including India and Southeast Asia with more than $10 billion in assets under management, has increased how much it invests per startup through Surge, its seed-stage investing platform, as it unveils a new cohort of 18 companies.

At least three of the companies in this cohort had already raised outside funding, in some cases from Peak XV itself, before joining Surge.

The new batch, called Surge 12, is the first to operate under Peak XV’s higher investment ceiling of up to $5 million per company, up from $3 million previously. The venture firm invested more than $50 million across the cohort, which has collectively raised over $90 million in seed funding, according to Peak XV. Its median investment per company has also increased, though the firm declined to disclose the figure.

“The bar to raise a Series A has gone up pretty significantly,” Rajan Anandan (pictured above), managing director at Peak XV, said in an interview. He added that the firm is also seeing more capital-intensive companies, particularly in deeptech, that are raising larger rounds at the seed stage.

Surge has become more global with each cohort, Anandan told TechCrunch, with its latest group spanning founders and companies from San Francisco to Sydney. Just five of the 18 startups in Surge 12 are focused on the Indian market, while more than half of the companies are based in India. The remaining 13 target global markets, highlighting the difference between where the companies are built and where they expect to find customers.

Since its launch in 2019, when Peak XV operated as Sequoia Capital India and Southeast Asia, Surge has backed more than 180 startups founded by entrepreneurs representing more than 18 nationalities. Peak XV says the 10 largest companies to emerge from those cohorts now generate more than $1 billion in combined annual revenue.

Surge founders at the Peak XV U.S. Immersion 2026Image Credits:Peak XV Partners

Anandan described Surge as Peak XV’s primary route for seed-stage investing, with the firm remaining an investor as companies progress through later funding rounds. The founders it backs typically include repeat entrepreneurs, experienced operators, and highly specialized technical founders, he said, with about 50% to 60% of a typical cohort made up of people coming from operating roles at established technology companies.

This cohort’s startups span AI, robotics, space, consumer products, healthcare, music, and fintech, ranging from AI safety and personal computing to autonomous robots built for underground pipes and satellites designed to detect radio-frequency signals from orbit.

The Surge 12 cohort

Alma — founded by Nischith Shadagopan M N and Vinod Ganesan — is building a personal computing platform focused on making computer use faster and more affordable. Its founders previously worked at Microsoft Research and were founding engineers at Sarvam AI, a Bengaluru-based startup building AI models for Indian languages.

August AI — founded by Anuruddh Mishra, an IIT-BHU alumnus who started the company in 2022 after a personal medical misdiagnosis — provides a healthcare platform that combines AI with physician-led care, reaching over 9 million users across 160 countries.

Ditto — founded by UC Berkeley dropouts Allen Wang and Eric Liu — works as an AI dating matchmaker inside iMessage, aimed at helping college students turn digital introductions into in-person connections. (TechCrunch wrote more about this one last month.) The company had already raised $9.2 million in a Peak XV-led seed round announced earlier this year.

GameStock — founded by Antoine Mistico, Easton Dana, and Vivek Indlebele Narasimha Prasad — brings competition mechanics to financial markets, turning investing and trading into a more competitive experience. Mistico is a two-time founder and former professional baseball player.

HiLoop — founded by Jad Ghalayini, Karan Brar, and Thomas Boser — helps AI companies adapt general-purpose open-weight models for specific applications using its post-training platform. Its founding team includes former Reducto engineers and a Cambridge computer science PhD who completed his doctorate at 24.

Hoola Health — founded by Deeksha Senguttuva — focuses on care for children and their families, providing consultations, vaccinations, medicines, diagnostics, developmental therapy, and dental services on a single platform. Senguttuvan grew up around healthcare, as her family built and operated a hospital group.

Kello — founded by Mona Gandhi and Subramanya Jingade — is building an AI-powered talent-discovery platform focused on identifying a candidate’s potential and trajectory rather than relying primarily on conventional credentials. Gandhi says she was Airbnb’s first female engineer and she previously founded Upraised, while Jingade previously co-founded AmbitionBox.

Kindling — founded by Adam Miller and Sachin Shah — is building what it calls a “storytelling operating system” for technology startups, using AI to help companies develop and produce their communications and content.

Puralink — founded by Harrison Crowe-Maxwell, Shyeon Delnawaz, and Thien “Long” Tran — is developing autonomous robots that can navigate underground pipe networks. Crowe-Maxwell has been building robots since childhood and turned university research into the patented drive technology behind the startup.

Reinforce Labs — founded by Anish Das Sarma — is developing tools to evaluate, red-team, and remediate enterprise AI systems. Sarma previously founded a company acquired by Airbnb and later served as a director at Google, where he led AI and machine-learning teams.

Riffle — founded by Anurag Choudhary and deo — is building a browser-based platform where musicians can create, collaborate on, and share music, reducing the need to move between separate tools during the creative process.

Rosella — founded by Chris Dwyer and Sean Stuart — is building an AI-native commercial insurance brokerage for U.S. businesses, using AI to automate parts of the traditionally manual process of finding and placing business insurance. Rosella raised a roughly $2.5 million pre-seed round led by Peak XV and Intact Private Capital earlier this year.

Tribe Money — founded by Himanshu Arora, Nikhil Shanker, and Aditya Varma — gives an AI-powered personal finance platform that helps users track their money, research investments and make investing decisions.

ULOOK — founded by Adheesh Boratkar and Siddhesh Ravindra Naik — is building autonomous satellite systems for radio-frequency sensing and spectrum intelligence, targeting customers globally. Its founders have worked on more than 12 satellite missions. The company had already raised roughly $2.3 million in seed funding from growX Ventures and InfoEdge Ventures before joining Surge.

Wingit — founded by Nikunj Kothari and Saksham Khandelwal — is building a beauty platform aimed at India’s growing premium-consumer market. It is focused on how consumers discover and shop for higher-end beauty products.

Three other startups in the cohort have yet to publicly reveal their names or products. Peak XV said they are working in education, applied AI, and medical products.

title: Microsoft launches 12-inch Surface Pro with Snapdragon X2 Plus & 5G, 13-inch Surface Laptop too
snippet: Microsoft is rolling out refreshes to its smaller Surface Laptop and Surface Pro machines powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Plus starting at a price of $1,149. more…
fullText:
Microsoft is rolling out refreshes to its smaller Surface Laptop and Surface Pro machines powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Plus starting at a price of $1,149.

The Surface Laptop and Surface Pro both picked up their Snapdragon X2 upgrades back in June, but that left the smaller models waiting on refreshes. As a part of Snapdragon Summit, Microsoft is confirming that those will arrive on October 13.

Surface Pro 12-inch is getting a Snapdragon X2 Plus chip, a 25% brighter display, and a battery that’s “30% more efficient.” There’s an optional 5G model coming too, which Microsoft says was “one of the most requested additions.” All models now include either 16GB or 24GB of RAM, removing the 8GB option on last year’s model, with either 256GB or 512GB of storage. 

It’s mostly the same tablet otherwise, just now with a starting price of $1,149. That’s $300 more than the base model sold for, and that’s after a major price hike across the whole lineup back in April. Even directly comparing the 16/256GB model, it’s still a $100 price hike. 

	

The formula is similar on Surface Laptop 13-inch, with this latest generation getting Snapdragon X2 Plus, ditching its 8GB model, and starting at $1,199 – $50 up from the last generation. Again, there are upgrades including a brigher display, but it’s nearly identical to last year’s model outside of the chipset bump.

Microsoft is also launching a new Surface Mouse which has haptic feedback and a customizable Copilot button. It costs $79.99 and will also be available on October 13. Both come with a new “Microsoft Ink Canvas” app.

title: Gemini app replacing Gems with skills in November
snippet: In 2024, Google introduced Gems as “custom versions of Gemini.” The Gemini app will soon replace Gems with “skills.” more…
fullText:
In 2024, Google introduced Gems as “custom versions of Gemini.” The Gemini app will soon replace Gems with “skills.”

Going to the Gems manager today reveals a new notice at the top: “Gems will become skills starting Nov 17, 2026.”

Starting November 17, 2026, we’ll automatically begin migrating your Gems to skills. You will be able to use your Gems until they migrate.

Google introduced skills with Gemini Spark, and they serve the same purpose as Gems at a high level. Both let you give Gemini custom instructions.

	
	

Gems let you go a step further by setting a default tool, like Create image or Canvas, and adding specific files for context. They can also be shared with other users via links.

That said, skills are more easily invoked with a / in the prompt box, while multiple can be used at the same time. This broader access is better than first having to go to Gems in the side panel and scrolling down for My Gems.

Google’s announcement might have rolled out slightly early as the “Learn more” help article and “Create skills” button do not work yet.

If you’re a Google AI Pro or AI Ultra subscriber, you can make skills by switching to the Gemini Spark tab. Typing a slash in the Chat box will let you use skills in the main conversational experience.

title: Apple Ordered to Pay $5.7 Billion for Infringing Haptics Patent in iPhone, Apple Watch
snippet: A jury awards Taction Technology damages over Apple’s use of vibration-based tactile technology in its devices.
fullText:
Apple has been ordered to pay $5.7 billion in damages for infringing on two patents owned by a gaming headset company. Taction Technology, which also supplied the tech found in the Corsair HS60 headset, alleged in 2021 that Apple infringed on two patents related to its haptics systems in its Apple Watch and iPhone.

The headset company’s complaint, which was heard before a jury in the District Court for the Southern District of California, alleged that Apple’s “Taptic Engine” was “capitalizing on Taction’s innovation and success.” Taction alleged that both systems used vibration-based, tactile transducer technology that helps users feel a device respond to their input, and argued that Apple used its inventions “without proper license or authority.” The jury agreed, but also found that Apple didn’t willfully infringe on the patents.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, but said it “strongly disagreed” with the verdict and said it will appeal the decision.

			

More from CNET

“Apple’s Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction’s technology, which Taction’s own testing of Apple’s products confirmed during trial. Apple does not use Taction’s technology, and we will appeal,” Apple told CNET.

Apple had originally won a dismissal of the action in 2023, but Taction Technology appealed.

The case follows a successful $634 million lawsuit brought by medical devices company Masimo, which alleged the Cupertino, California-based company used Masimo’s proprietary monitoring technology in the Apple Watch.

Apple, as one of the largest consumer electronics brands in the world, was briefly valued at $5 trillion in July. The company earlier this month replaced CEO Tim Cook with Apple’s former senior vice president John Ternus and unveiled its first folding iPhone.

Apple has been ordered to pay $5.7 billion in damages for infringing on two patents owned by a gaming headset company. Taction Technology, which also supplied the tech found in the Corsair HS60 headset, alleged in 2021 that Apple infringed on two patents related to its haptics systems in its Apple Watch and iPhone.

The headset company’s complaint, which was heard before a jury in the District Court for the Southern District of California, alleged that Apple’s “Taptic Engine” was “capitalizing on Taction’s innovation and success.” Taction alleged that both systems used vibration-based, tactile transducer technology that helps users feel a device respond to their input, and argued that Apple used its inventions “without proper license or authority.” The jury agreed, but also found that Apple didn’t willfully infringe on the patents.

title: Meta launches audio-only glasses and Gen 3 Ray-Ban with slimmer designs
snippet: Meta today introduced its new Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) smart glasses with a slimmer design and longer battery life alongside a new audio-only lineup, and a new $250 entry-level release. more…
fullText:
Meta today introduced its new Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) smart glasses with a slimmer design and longer battery life alongside a new audio-only lineup, and a new $250 entry-level release.

Despite public backlash in recent months, smart glasses continue to explode in popularity and, as it stands, Meta is by far the biggest player in the game. Today’s event further saw the company digging in on its smart glasses success with three new releases.

The self-branded Meta Glasses lineup is adding new styles that start at just $249. A new pair of Meta Adventurer glasses will be available with a black frame and grey lenses and a plug-in case. They’re available starting October 23. 

Next in line is a pair of audio-only glasses, Ray-Ban Meta Audio. Starting at $349 in October, these glasses ditch the camera and, in turn, also deliver a much slimmer form factor. They weigh 43g and run for 12 hours on a single charge (48 hours in the case). Meta says the new hardware features “professional-adjustable temple tips, adjustable or swappable nose pads, and overextension hinges.” 

	

Styles include “Clubmaster” and “Burbank” in a variety of frame and lens styles.

Beyond that, Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) is available today starting at $449. Meta says to expect longer battery life – 9 hours, an hour longer than Gen 2 – and the same camera capabilities, including 3K video recording. The hardware is slimmer and adds professional-adjustable temple tips. 

Meta is also launching this latest generation in way more styles, with 27 combinations across “Aviator,” “Wayfarer,” and cateye “Zena” frame styles.

You can order Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) now through Meta’s store.

Finally, Meta is also upgrading its Display glasses with hands-free navigation, “Hologram” personas for video calls, new apps, notification mirroring from your phone, and Threads integration. Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are also expanding to the UK, Canada, France, Italy, and Germany, and you can finally order them online in the US, still priced at $799.

title: Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-6 Sol & Luna both launch today with lower costs
snippet: Anthropic and OpenAI are both launching new model updates today, with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol & Luna both being announced within roughly an hour of each other. more…
fullText:
Anthropic and OpenAI are both launching new model updates today, with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol & Luna both being announced within roughly an hour of each other.

Claude Opus 5.5 was up to bat first today, so we’ll start there. 

Anthropic explains that its latest model update performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on “most work” while cutting costs to run by around 40% compared to Opus 5 – which was already around half the price of Fable 5. 

Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that. Our tests show that at default settings it will cost 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads. Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5. Cache reads (which make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs) are $0.20 per million tokens, 60% less than Opus 5. Opus 5.5 also generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.

Despite the lower compute costs, Anthropic says that Opus 5.5 is more powerful, beating out Fable 5.1 in every metric and beating OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra in virtually every category measured as well including metrics such as agentic coding, knowledge work, and more. 

	

Claude Opus 5.5 is available now on “all platforms,” Anthropic says.

And that’s not all. OpenAI, roughly an hour after Claude’s announcement, launched its GPT-6 Sol & Luna models, also focused on costs.

Like Opus 5.5, OpenAI says that GPT-6 Sol and Luna are both much more affordable to run compared to their GPT-5.6 counterparts. Specifically, they’re both about 50% less expensive when measuring input and output per 1 million tokens in API use. 

Both models are marginally more powerful than their predecessors, but well behind that of Astra, which remains the overall most powerful model OpenAI offers. Luna prioritizes cost over capability, while Sol strikes a balance between the two by offering more horsepower than Luna but at a more affordable cost compared to Astra.

We trained GPT‑6 Sol and Luna with similar methods as GPT‑6 Astra, bringing the advances behind Astra’s state-of-the-art performance in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable models.

The GPT‑6 models lead across the cost–intelligence curve, combining exceptional capabilities at every tier with infrastructure that delivers them efficiently at scale. Improvements in caching and inference let us serve these models at lower cost, and we’re passing those savings directly on to users and customers by reducing API prices for Sol and Luna by 50% compared with their GPT‑5.6 promotional pricing.

OpenAI says Sol and Luna are available in ChatGPT Work and Codex starting today for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users, while Luna is available in the desktop app for Free and Go users. Neither model is available in Chat just yet.

title: AeroPress Unveils a Coffee Press Made of Luscious Walnut Wood
snippet: The portable travel press just got an all-natural makeover.
fullText:
Ahead of National Coffee Day on Tuesday and following the release of a stainless steel version of its iconic coffee press, AeroPress released its walnut collection, marking the first time the company has launched a wood design. 

Known for its three-in-one brew method that combines immersion like a French press, aeration like a pour-over and air pressure like an espresso machine to give you your java in under two minutes, AeroPress’s walnut collection is an extension of the brand’s premium line and includes both a brewer and a manual grinder in solid, clear-grade walnut. 

Why walnut?

A representative for AeroPress told CNET that because the brewer and grinder are tactile products, the company has been interested in using wood for quite some time. They settled on walnut for its warm tone that contrasts nicely with the final design’s darker finishes.

			

More from CNET

A warm walnut was chosen to complement the new darker finishes.AeroPress

What else has changed? 

Like the other brewers in the premium collection, the walnut version is still made of 304 stainless steel, aluminum and double-wall borosilicate glass with laser-etched measurement markings. 

However, the AeroPress representative said that the brewer’s chamber had to be completely redesigned to accommodate the walnut accent. So did the plunger, flange, scoop and stir accessories, all of which are made of solid wood. 

What the walnut collection looks like on my own countertop.Anna Gragert/CNET

As for the 25-gram-capacity grinder that has over 60 grind settings, AeroPress gave its arm a new black finish and its handle a walnut makeover, while the overall body now has a darker tone. The catch’s metal component was designed to fit a solid walnut sleeve. It also has Italian-made, titanium-coated 38-millimeter conical burrs with a lifetime warranty, dual bearings, a patent-pending Easy-Grind system and a removable magnetic handle that allows the grinder to be easily stored inside the AeroPress itself. 

A closer look at the grounds inside the grinder.Anna Gragert/CNET

Being able to store both the grinder and its handle inside the AeroPress brewer is a first-of-its-kind design for the company. 

My partner, who is more of a coffee person than I am, said the walnut collection both looks and feels high-quality. And that it brews a delicious cup of coffee. 

I especially love the grinder’s walnut handle, which has a lovely feel.Anna Gragert/CNET

Sustainability

When asked about sustainability, the AeroPress representative said that the walnut used in the new design is grown in the USA and sourced from responsibly managed forests. 

“For us, sustainability is also about durability and longevity,” the representative added. “Everything we make, including our walnut line, is designed to last, and we offer replacement parts for key components so products can be repaired rather than replaced.”

The walnut is sourced from responsibly managed forests in the USA.Anna Gragert/CNET

Price and availability

In addition to being repairable, the walnut collection was designed with the countertop — not the inside of the cabinet — in mind. The brewer and grinder each cost $250 for a total of $500 and are now available on AeroPress.com and Williams-Sonoma.com.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Anna Gragert
						

						

							Senior Editor, Health and Home						
					

											

								

											Anna Gragert (she/her/hers) was previously the lifestyle editor at HelloGiggles, the deputy editor at So Yummy and the senior lifestyle editor at Hunker. Over the past 12 years, Anna has also written for the LA Times, Elle, Bust Magazine, Dazed, Apartment Therapy, Well+Good and more. At CNET, she's a senior editor on the Healthy Home team, and her coverage includes health, wellness tech, meal kits and home and kitchen tech with a focus on the technology that aims to help us live our healthiest, happiest lives.

snippet: As part of Made on YouTube 2026, a handful of updates to YouTube Music that are coming later this year were previewed. more…
fullText:
As part of Made on YouTube 2026, a handful of updates to YouTube Music that are coming later this year were previewed.

After moving search to the bottom bar earlier this year, YouTube Music is placing the Gemini spark icon in the top-right corner of the mobile app to let you access Ask Music. This more consistent entry point — compared to the Home feed card — slides up a sheet with the chat experience. 

The prompt box is at the bottom of the screen with voice input available, while suggested queries include Create a mix, Discover artists, and Find podcasts. 

Ask Music will also be surfaced throughout YouTube Music when relevant, like when you’re editing a playlist or creating a mix. The conversational tool is also adding more agentic features this year that let you “customize your queue or dive deeper into artist lore.”

	

These updates are coming later this year for global YouTube Premium and Music Premium subscribers.

The other YouTube Music update today is a “Your Podcast Lineup” feature that acts as a “personalized AI-audio guide.” It gives you a “weekly spoken preview of recommended shows” that includes why you might like them, as well as suggested episodes. 

This “completely eyes-optional and hands-free” experience leverages audio gen AI capabilities. Testing will start later this year for subscribers worldwide.

title: Galaxy S27 Ultra’s missing camera shown in leaks is its 3x zoom
snippet: Previous Galaxy S27 Ultra leaks have directed attention to the new camera island, but don’t overlook the missing camera lens left behind with the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Apparently, that camera is the Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra’s 10MP 3x zoom. more…
fullText:
Previous Galaxy S27 Ultra leaks have directed attention to the new camera island, but don’t overlook the missing camera lens left behind with the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Apparently, that camera is the Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra’s 10MP 3x zoom.

We’ve seen a selection of leaks with details galore, including privacy displays, battery upgrades, and more. Any render that’s come out has shown off an entirely new camera island design, and it’s become the focus of the new phone. Love it or hate it, it’s there and almost square.

According to another leak via @UniverseIce on Twitter/X, the Galaxy S27 Ultra won’t have a 3x optical zoom lens with a 10MP sensor. Instead, the phone will have a wide 1x lens setup and a 5x optical zoom unit – 50MP, if left unchanged as suggested.

It is now confirmed that the Galaxy S27 Ultra will no longer have a 3× telephoto camera.

This means its rear camera system will jump directly from the 1× main camera to the 5× telephoto camera.

The main camera uses the ISOCELL HP6, essentially a Galaxy-customized version of the… https://t.co/qYGcdX93oy

— Ice Universe (@UniverseIce) September 29, 2026

The latest renders clearly show a missing lens if you compare the phone to last year’s model. The Galaxy S26 Ultra had a 3x and 5x optical zoom camera, totaling four sensors across the back of the phone. Now, sitting in a section of much larger real estate, the new camera array appears to have only three cameras.

	

A render posted by @OnLeaks labels portions of the new panel. Where previous renders showed another lens underneath the flash LED, this new render places the LED at the bottom, topped by additional sensors, a microphone, and what may now be the 5x zoom lens.

As is the case with nearly every Galaxy S series leak, these are to be taken with a grain of salt. Renders have come and gone, but we won’t know the final details until Samsung launches the device sometime in early 2027.
